OBSERVATION/CONCLUSION AND RECOMMENDATION OF THE COMMITTEE 
The Committee observes that main object ofthe Coal India (Regulation of Transfers and 
Validation) Bill, 1995 is to empower the Central Government to direct the transfer of land, on the 
rights in or over or of the right, title and interest in relation to a Coal Mine, Coking Coal Mine or 
Coke Oven Plant, vested in Coal India Limited or in a subsidiary company to any subsidiary 
company and to validate certain transfers of such land or sights. Speaking on practical terms, the 
proposed legislation simply aims at legalisations of transfers of properties from Coal India 
Limited to its subsidiaries and that too without vitiating the managing and controlling mechanism 
of Coal India Limited over its subsidiaries. The Bill aims at turning the situation from de facto to 
de jure. De facto transfer of property has already taken place through administrative orders. 
2. The Committee feels that the necessity of the proposed enactment arose due to 
shortcomings in the Coal Nationalisation Act, under which provision was made for taking over 
all the mines by the Central Government, not by Coal India. Under that Act, Government was 
given the power to transfer it to the Government Company, which was done to erstwhile CMAL 
and now Coal India Limited. There was no provision in the Nationalisation Act for second 
transfer from Coal India to its subsidiaries which have already been done through administrative 
order. Therefore, the proposed legislation is a validation legislation for enabling the Government 
to provide -legal basis to a defacto transfer and convert the same into de-jure. 
3. The Committee understands the problem of giving validation to the transfer of properties 
through the Coal Nationalisation Validation Act, because, unfortunately, the properties of Coal 
India today, which are sought to be transferred to the subsidiaries, are not all covered by the 
nationalization scheme, that is so, because the Coal Mines Nationalisation Act had a very specific 
schedule attached to the Act which designated the mines that were to be taken over. It is 
noteworthy that there are other transfer of properties under the Coal-~earing, Act and the Land 
Acquisition Act, which would still not be covered. The same transfer couldn't be done through 
the Transfer of property Act because the said Act allows only prospective transfer. So, the 
Committee is of the view that the only way to clear up the mess of ownership is to bring forth a 
separate legislation. 
4. The Committee notes the Opinion/suggestion of Shri Lal Narayan Sinha, former 
Attorney General (who was defending the case in the Supreme Court on behalf of BCCL) and 
then Attorney General, Shri K. Parasnath, who endorsed the view of Shri Lal Narayan Sinha for 
undertaking the recourse for appropriate legislation so that, as on date, whatever is held by 
subsidiaries, could be transferred to them without involving any legal wrangle. 
5. The Committee understands that CIL have created a structure of subsidiaries but the 
subsidiaries had not been transferred the property in legal sense, therefore, existing structure of 
arrangement may lead to some kind of problem in future. The problem occurred in Bharat 
Coking Coal Ltd. VS Government of Bihar and others and the Supreme Court decided the 
matter. However, the question of de-jure possession of the properties by the Coal companies and 
the rights and liabilities that go with it remained unresolved which is intended to be cured by the 
proposed legislation. 
6. The Committee, while examining the points of objections raised by the Governments of 
Assam and Bihar on the present Bill and the comments of the Ministry of Coal, is ofthe view that 
the Ministry of Coal has successfully clarified the points of objections of both the state 
Governments. The Committee observes that the lands, titles etc. vested in Coal Mines Authority 
Ltd/Coal India Ltd. following nationalization of Coal Mines in 1973 which provided for deemed 
9 

lease require no formal execution of mining lease under Mines and Minerals (Regulation & 
Development) Act, 1957 and Mineral Concession Rules, 1960. 
7. The Committee is also of the opinion that since Section 3 of the Coal Mines 
(Nationalisation) Act, 1973 transfers and vests the right, title and interest of the Coal Mines in 
the Central Government free from all encumbrances and Section-S( I) of the said Act has vested 
the right, title, interest etc., of the Coal Mines with the CIL and because these are nationalized 
properties, the transfer of these properties from CIL to a subsidiary or from one subsidiary to 
another subsidiary of the CIL, does not harm the interest of the State(s). 
8. The Committee endorses the view that the proposed enactment overrides the Acts of 
State Legislature namely Bihar Tenancy Act, Chhotanagpur Tenancy Act, Santhal Parganas 
Tenancy Act because, it flows from the Coal Mines (Nationalisation ) Act and Section-28 of the 
Coal Nationalisation Act has an overriding provision stipulating that the Nationalisation Act shall 
have effect notwithstanding anything in consisting therewith in any other law for the time being 
in force. 
9. The Committee also notes and endorses the contention of the Ministry of Coal that since 
the acquisition of Mines by the Central Government under the Nationalisation Act is not as a 
,.result of the actual grant by the state as done under Minerals Concession Rules (MCR}, 1960 
framed under MMRD Act. 1957 but by a legal fiction and also because Section-28 of the 
Nationalisation Act, 1973 having an overriding effect in terms of which where there is conflict 
between the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973 and MMRD Act and MCR framed there 
under, then the provision of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973 wHI override the 
provisions of MMRD Act. etc., therefore, the question that the proposed enactment violates the 
provision of MMRD Act and MCR does not arise. 
10. During the course of oral-evidence of Secretaries to the Department of Legislation 
(Ministry of Law Justice and Company Affairs) and the Ministry of Coal, the Committee got an 
assurance that the Bill will not dilute the control of Coal India over the subsidiaries. The 
Secretary, Coal, assured that the Bill will do nothing to dilute the Government's ownership of 
either the Coal India or the subsidiaries i.e., the control of Government over the subsidiaries 
would be as complete as of Coal India. Under the Article, of Association of Subsidiary 
Companies, the Subsidiary Companies cannot do certain things without the approval from Coal 
India e.g., it cannot dispose of a substantial part of its assets without approval from Coal India 
neither the majo'r investment decision of the subsidiaries can be done without the approval of 
Coal·lndia. The Articles of Association also says that, if the subsidiary is going to a foreign 
company or going in for a joint venture, it has to go "in and through" the Coal lndia.The 
Committee is satisfied with the explanation of the Migistry of Coal and the Ministry of Law, 
Justice and Company Affairs (Legislative Depart!}lellt). 
11. Having heard the Secretaries.__ Ministry of Coal and Legislative Department, Ministry of 
Law Justice and Company Affairs and the clarifications given by them to the various queries and 
having considered the papers furnished by the Ministry, the Committee agrees* with the proposal 
of the Ministry to empower the Central Government to direct the transfer of the land or of the 
right, title and interest in relation to a coal mine, coking coal mine or coke oven plant, vested in 
the Coal India Limited or in subsidiary company to any subsidiary company of Coal India 
Limited or any other subsidiary company and to validate certain transfers of such land or rights. 
12. The Committee decided to adopt Clause 2, 3 & 4 in the original form. 
13. Clause 1 i.e., the Enacting Formula and the Title, were adopted, with changes of 
consequential nature, namely, "1995 and Forty-Sixth" to be substituted by "2000" and Fifty-first, 
respectively. 
10 

14. The Committee therefore, recommends the Coal India (Regulation of Transfers and 
Validation) Bill, 1995 as amended to the Parliament for adoption.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS 
The coal industry was nationalised in two phases, that is, in 1972 and· 1973. After 
nationalisation, the coking and non-coking coal mines in the Jharia CoalFields in Bihar and a few 
mines in Barakar and Mugma regions were directed to be vested in the Bharat Coking Coal 
Limited, Dhanbad. Most of the other coal mines in the States of Assam, Bihar, West Bengal, 
Orissa, Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra were directed to be vested in the Coal Mines Authority 
Limited. Subsequently, a holding company, namely, the Coal1ndia Limited was set up with effect 
from the 1st November, 1975, initially with five subsidiaries. Later three more subsidiaries were 
created by del inking certain collieries from other subsidiaries. 
2. Ever since the nationalisation of the coal industry, though the land or rights in or over such land 
acquired under various Acts and the right, title and interest in relation to a coal mine or a coke 
oven plant were directed to be \lested in the Coal India Limited or its predecessor in title, its 
subsidiary companies were de facto managing such land, coal mines or plants. 
3. The absence of a formal legal title to the land or rights in or over such land or the right, title and 
interest in relation to a coal mine or coke oven plant, in the subsidiary companies has exposed 
them to litigation and other legal infirmities. While the Companies Act, 1956 contains provisions 
for reconstruction and amalgamations, such reconstruction or amalgamation could be given effect 
to prospectively only under that Act. 
4. It has, therefore, been considered necessary to empower the Central Government to direct the 
transfer of land or the rights in or over such land or the right, title or interest in relation to a coal 
mine or coke oven plant vested in the Coal India Limited to a subsidiary company, or where such 
land or mine are vested in a subsidiary company, to another subsidiary company. It has also been 
considered necessary to validate all purported transfers of the land or rights in or over such land or 
the right, title and interest in relation to a coal mine or coke oven plant from the Coal India 
Limited to a subsidiary company and from one subsidiary company to another subsidiary company 
before the commencement of the proposed legislation. 
5. The Bill seeks to achieve the above objects.

and thereafter, decided to have interaction with officials of the Ministry of Small Scale 
Industries and Agro & Rural Industries, RBI!Banks/Financial Institutions/KVIC and 
representatives of SSI Association and NGOs to assess the impact of the policy/package on the

REPORT 
Small Scale Industries Sector plays paramount role in the National economy and has 
vast potential in terms of employment, output, export promotion, expansion of base for 
indigenous entrepreneurship and decentralization of industries in rural areas. The number of 
persons employed in the SSI sector was 171.58 lakhs while the production of the sector at 
current prices was Rs.5,27,515 crore produced in more than 3 million units. The SSI sector 
export performance has been of the order of Rs.48,979 crores. In this respect the achievement 
of growth in SSI sector has been 7. 7. per cent in 1998-99 compared to 4 per cent growth in the 
industrial sector. The Employment growth between 1998-99 has been of the order of 2.62 
percent over previous year which has been better than the overall growth in the employment 
of around I per cent. The sector has exceeded the employment target in 81h Five Year Plan and 
the achievement in the Ninth Five Year Plan is satisfactory in this regard with a growth rate 
around 4 per cent per year. 
During the course of examination of Demand for Grants (2000-0 1) pertaining to the 
Ministry of Small Scale Industry and Agro & Rural Industries, the Department Related 
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry took up the issue of credit flow to SSI Sector in 
detail. It was informed to the Committee by the Secretary that the problematic area in the sector 
is about SSI credit, as percentage of net banking credit was about 16 per cent, in March, 1996 
which went up to 17.33 per cent in March, 1999. In absolute terms, the credit to the SSI sector 
has increased to Rs.42,674 crores in March, 1999 which is a significant improvement, compared 
with the figure of Rs.30,000 crores il'l March, 1996. However, the disturbing feature is that the 
amount of credit to the tiny sector is not adequate. But at the end of March, 1999, the tiny sector 
got a credit of Rs.8,837.47 crores which is about 20.7 per cent of the credit going to the SSI 
sector and as per the norms laid down by the RBI, 60 per cent of the SSI credit should have gone 
to the tiny sector. It is this reason which has prompted to launch the Credit Guarantee Scheme. 
Moreover the RBI had advised the banks to introduce special branches for the small scale sector 
and 3 89 branches have already been set lip. The banks have also been directed by Ministry of 
Finance to enhance the coverage of Small Scale Industries branches to individual districts. 
Apart from this, SIDBI has introduced Single Window Scheme for working capital and term 
loans. Since the Small Scale Industries sector is facing the problem because of absence of 
working capital loans in time and in case ifthe same institution will be responsible for both term 
loans and working capital, the situation will improve. 
The Committee was informed during examination of Demands for Grants (2000-200 1) 
that in order to improve the credit flow to Small Scale Industries the Credit Guarantee Scheme 
has been launched during the year 2000-2001. This' provides for contribution to a fund to 
generate loans without any collateral. The scheme will be implemented jointly by the Central 
Government and Small Industries Development Bank of India through a trust. The funds required 
for the scheme will be provided by Government of India and SIDBI in the ratio of 4: 1. SIDBI is 
also presently administrating the technology development and modernisation funds scheme for 
assisting technological development and modernisation of Small Scale Industries units. This 
scheme has certain concessional features including interest at prime lending rate for direct 
assistance for improving the credit flow. In past also RBI had issued instruction that out of funds 
normally available to Small Scale Industries sector, 40% would be given to the units with 
investment in Plan and machinery up to Rs.S lakhs, 20% to the unit with investment between Rs.S 
lakhs and 25 lakhs and remaining 40% for other units. The single window scheme of SIDBI has 
also been extended to all the districts.

not entertain new entrepreneurs and not even provided the application forms. New exporters with 
confirm orders do not get the opportunity to even open a bank account.

The Committee came to know that despite of the various schemes and instructions the 
credit flow against the target of 60% for tiny sector the actual flow has been only 20.71%. 
The Committee in its 40th Report felt that if the banks were able to achieve the target 
of 60% of creqit to tiny sector, the contribution of Small Scale Industries Sector would have been 
much higher as it stands now. The Committee in that Report had the recommended that effort 
should be made to achieve the target of 60%.The Committee also noted that the Net Bank 
Credit is Rs.2,46,203 crore and credit to Small Scale Industries Sector is Rs.42,674 crore at the 
end of March, 1999 i.e. only 17% of finance to the Small Scale Industries Sector which is 
contributing 35% in exports and the aggregated value of production of Small Scale Industries 
sector in 1998-99 was Rs. 5,27,515 crore. The Committee therefore recommended in its 40th 
Report that banks and other financial institutions should meet the fund requirement of Small 
Scale Industries Sector by providing them more lending facilities so that they can contribute more 
to the economy. 
The Ministz of SSI and A&RI in its Action Taken notes on the recommendation 
contained in the 401 Report stated that the issue was taken up ~ith the RBI who have informed 
that the flow of credit to SSI Sector has shown a steady increase over the years. The advances of 
the Public Sector Banks to SSI Sector have gone up considerably from Rs.l6, 783 crore in March, 
1991 to Rs.42,674 crores in March, 1999 constituting 17.3% of the Net Bank Credit. Many 
measures taken as a follow up of the Nayak Committee and Kapur Committee recommendations 
and the policies initiated by the Government have resulted in the increase in the credit flow. 
Further, the recent instructions issued to Banks for raising the exemption limit for non-obtention

and the policies initiated by the Government have resulted in the increase in the credit flow. 
Further, the recent instructions issued to Banks for raising the exemption limit for non-obtention 
of collateral securities from Rs.l lakh to Rs.5 lakhs, raising the limit of composite loans from 
Rs.5 lakhs to Rs.l 0 lakhs, opening of specialised SSI branches in each District, etc., would 
provide more lending facilities to the SSI Sector. The new scheme of Credit Guarantee Fund and 
the proposed scheme of credit linked capital subsidy for Technology upgradation are expected to 
improve the flow of credit to the SSI sector. 
The Committee in its 40th report outlined the general perception that SIDBI has a 
number of good schemes, their reach is inadequate as most of the schemes are routed through 
primary lending institutions. There has been mixed response whether SIDBI, an Apex 
institution, as hitherto, should confine largely to providing resource support to intermediaries for 
implementation of various schemes and programmes, or should do more of direct retail lending. 
Given the structure and stature of SIDBI, it is largely expected to play a role of the Apex Bank 
providing resource support to the PLis and initiating appropriate developmental programme for 
the healthy growth of Small Scale Industries. Its direct lending has been specifically in those 
areas where PLis have been shy in assisting the units or in high risk areas such as infrastructure, 
marke.ting, venture financing etc. Therefore, the Committee recommended that SIDBI should 
take initiative and act as a watch dog to monitor the activities of Indian and Foreign Banks. 
Being mainly for the small scale sector, it would be appropriate if SIDBI is placed under the 
administrative control of Ministry of Small Scale Industries and Agro & Rural Industries. 
Replying to the recommendation contained in the 40th report the Ministry of SSI and A&RI 
informed the Committee that the issue was taken up with the SIDBI and Banking Division, 
Ministry of Finance. The SIDBI has endorsed the view that there is need for adequate provision 
to the SIDBI to monitor the activity of Primary Lending Institutions (including Indian and 
Foreign Banks) with regard to their assistance and policies towards SSI Sector. This is 
necessary keeping in view the coordination role envisaged from the SIDBI in terms of SIDBI 
Act 1989. Banking Division, Ministry of Finance has also endorsed the views ofthe SIDBI. 
The matter regarding, placing SIDBI under the Administrative Control of Ministry of 
(SSI and A&R ) was also taken up with the Banking Division, Ministry of Finance and the 
SIDBI. The SIDBI, is of the view that good coordination exists between the SIDBI and Ministry 
of SSI and A&RI with regard to framing suitable policy guidelines and programmes for the 
benefit of SSis. However, as far as Administrative control of the SIDBI is concerned, keeping in 
view that the SIDBl is primarily an All-India Financial Institution and the Administrative control 
of Banks/ All-India Financial Institution is with the Ministry of Finance it would be appropriate if 
the SIDBI continues to be under the Administrative control of the Ministry of Finance. Banking 
Division, Ministry of Finance has also endorsed the views of SIDBI. SIDBI is primarily a 
refinancing agency. In the interest of proper linking of SIDBI with financial and monetary 
policy, it is essential that the SIDBI should continue under the Ministry of Finance. Secretary 
(SSI and A&RI) is already a member of the Board of Directors and DC (SSI) in the National 
Advisory Committee. DC (SSI) is also a member in the Board of Trustees of Credit Guarantee 
Trust Fund which has been created for running the Credit Guarantee Fund Scheme. D{: (SSI) is 
also a member in SIDBI's Committee on Micro Credit. 
The issue of credit/loan disbursement by foreign banks was examined in the 
Committees 40th Report wherein it is stated that the job of giving loan to entrepreneurs mainly 
rests with Nationalised Banks. All scheduled commercial banks and banks in private sector 
should give 40% of their lending to Private sector. To give support to foreign banks and the 
private sector banks there is a provision that if there is a shortfall in the priority sector lending, 
which include Small Scale Industries, tiny industries, beneficiaries of PMRY and other things, 
they <.;an deposit that shortfall. The private sector is with NABARD and the foreign banks with

SIDBI. The foreign banks found it more convenient to deposit this amount with SIDBI rather 
than disburse it. Thus, the priority sector lending objective is not fulfilled by foreign banks. As 
intimated by the Ministry, as a group, foreign banks have achieved the target of 10% of net bank 
credit stipulated in the case of lending to SSI sector. However, some individual banks have not 
achieved the target. As per the existing rules, foreign banks which report shortfalls in lending to 
the priority sector or the sub-sectors (SSI & Export) are required to place deposits equivalent to

Considering the importance of Small Scale Industries for national economic development 
and growth the Govt. of India has accorded high priority to this sector. Hon'ble Prime Minister, 
Shri Atal Bihari Vajpayee, announced on 30th August, 2000 special package for SSI. The policy

(i) The loan limit under composite Loan Scheme would be enhanced from Rs.1 0 lakhs to

lakhs will qualify for priority lending.

The Committee interacted with the representatives of Khadi and Village Industries 
Commission (KVIC) and came to know that Khadi and Village Industries have the unique 
capacity to generate large employment opportunities in the rural areas at a low capital cost and 
have therefore occupied an important place in the national economy. These industries develop 
local initiatives, cooperation and spirit of self-reliance in the economy and at the same time 
help in utilisation of available manpower for processing local available raw materials by 
adoption of simple techniques. The functions of the KVIC are generally to plan, promote and 
assist in implementation of programmes for the development of Khadi and Village Industries. 
To achieve this, it undertakes (a) financing of eligible agencies, (b) training of persons employed 
or desirous of seeking employment of in Khadi and Village Industries (c) supply of 
tools/equipment, (d) R&D in Khadi and Village Industries sector, (e) promotion to sale and 
marketing of Khadi and Village Industries products. (f) promotion and encouragement of 
cooperative efforts among the persons engaged in Khadi and Village Industries etc. The 
different sources of finance available for development programme for KVIC are, in addition to 
the funds released by Government of India under budgetary source, are funds drawn from 
consortium Bank credit and funds drawn by the beneficiaries from the Banks under ISEC 
scheme and Margin Money Scheme. KVIC is extending financial assistance to implementing 
agencies in the form of grant and loan for Khadi and Village Industries activities from budgetary 
sources and CBC fund. Additional funds are also mobilized for Khadi and polyester under 
ISEC scheme from institutional financial sources for viable projects of village industry under 
Margin Money Scheme. 
The Committee was informed that the Budgetary source fund for the activities of the 
KVIC are provided by the Central Government viz. Ministry of SSI and A&RI are in the form 
of plan and non-plan expenditure. Moreover, the some funds are provided by the Ministry of 
Non-Conventional Energy Sources. These funds are provided by way of grants and loans and 
the Commission re-allocates them to implementing agencies, namely the State KVIC Boards, 
societies registered under the Societies Registration Act. 1860 and cooperative societies 
registered under the Cooperative Act. of the state Governments. The major portion of the grant

(ISEC) was introduced by Government of India in 1978. Under the Scheme, implementing 
agencies can avail of bank loan as recommended by KVIC and they are required to pay only 4 
percent of interest and difference between interest charged by the Banks on the amount 
recommended by KVIC and the 4 percent is borne by KVIC. Upto 1999-2000 Bank loans 
under the scheme had reached to the level of Rs.362.23 crores. However, there is a gap in 
actual fund required under the ISEC by the Institutions i.e. the level of Interest Subsidy 
Eligibility Certificate issued by KVIC and actual funds released by the Banks to the Institutions 
under the scheme.

The representative of All India Association of Industries submitted a note on the 
"Financial Requirement of Small Scale Industry Sector in India" which highlights that the 
credit needs of Small Scale Industries are basically of two types i.e. long term loans and 
working capital . The working group on SSI for the Ninth Five Year Plan (1997-2002) 
estimated a long term credit requirement for the sector at Rs.345-365 billion and working 
capital funds at a level of Rs.l420-1460 billion, at 1997-98 prices. While the requirement of 
term loan for the sector is, by and large, being fulfilled by the financial institutions, the 
working capital requirement is not fully met leading to a credit gap situation. 
As regard the quantum of credit flow to SSI sector the Committee has been informed 
that the institutional source for SSI sector funding are operating in the country at the 
National and the State level . Apex level financial institution are Small Industrit"' 
Development Bank of India, Commercial Banks (CBs), Regional Rural Banks (RRB), 
Cooperative Banks (State Central and primary ) while State level Institutions are State 
Financi~l Corporations (SFCs), State Industrial Development Corporations (SIDC) , State 
Industrial Inves~ment Corporations (SIICs) and State Small Industries Development 
Corporation (SSIDCs) . Besides the National and State level institutions there are some 
other agencies like National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD), 
Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC) , National Small Scale Industries

The Note on the "Financial Requirements of Small Scale Industry Sector in India" 
highlights the problem pertaining to the ct:edit facilities to small scale sector by the banks 
which are as under:-
(i) Though the overall availability of credit from Commercial Banks to small scale 
industries has improved in absolute terms from Rs.179 .40 billion in March, 1991 
toRs. 515.85 billion in March, 1999, the availability of working capital credit 
in relation to annual turnover of SSis has not shown any significant 
improvement. The Nayak Committee found it to be 8.1 percent in 1990-91 and 
it stands at 8-9 percent even now. After a gap of I 0 years after the issuance of 
necessary guidelines by the RBI to improve the situation in this regard, nothing 
much has happened . 
(ii) Increase in the availability of bank credit to SSI sector is not commensurate to 
the increase in the productivity of this sector. For instance during the last ten 
years whereas the SSI production increased by 3.4 times the credit availability by 
the banks to the units increased by 2.9 times only. 
(iii) In spite of the RBI guidelines that 60 percent of the SSI credit should go to tiny 
sector, the quantum of credit to the sector as a percentage of SSI credit has been 
declining in recent years. 
(iv) It has been observed that most of the SSis do not take recourse to institutional 
credit on account of numerous factors. A study conducted by the Office of the 
DC (SSI) revealed that only 14 to 15 percent of SSI units avail bank finance 
This may be due to comprehensive conditions prescribed by the banks.

(v) The most important inhibitive factor for SSis availing bank finance is the 
insistence of collateral security that may be 2 to 3 times higher than the amount 
of loan required. Even if entrepreneurs are successful in meeting collateral 
requirements, they find it difficult to arrange third party guarantees as required 
by banks. 
(vi) The term loan and working capital requirements are not met by one single 
agency particularly if the loan requirement is for higher amount (above Rs.l 
million ). As a result, there is a gap in the sanction of two types of loans and 
mostly there is no mechanism for joint appraisal by term lending agency (SFC) 
and agencies meeting working capital requirements (banks). Further, most of 
the SFCs which meet the term loan needs of SSis are having rather weak 
financial base/support. 
(vii) Though specialised bank branches have been set up, the experience has shown 
that they are inclined to finance the large SSis only and try to avoid the 
smaller. 
(viii) The cost of credit in India is high and in case of SSis, it works out to be still 
higher because the criterion of fixing the rate of interest above the prime-lending 
rate is the credit worthiness. The credit worthiness of SSis is rather poor as 
compared to large units. The SSis in fact have to compete for credit with the 
larger units, a situation which for obvious reasons is to their disadvantage . 
(ix) There is no incentive in supply of credit for promoting technology upgradation 
and modernisation which is the need of the hour in the context of economic 
reforms, liberalization, globalization and due to the emergence of the WTO 
regulations. 
(x) The banks lack inducement to advance small loans due to high risk involved , 
lot of paper work, and high processing cost, high rate of sickness and NPAs in 
the SSI sector. 
(xi) Indian SSI sector has no access to capital market or foreign capital. The equity 
cap of24 percent is not sufficient to encourage foreign investment in a big way. 
In the light of the above analysis the future credit policy for SSI sector should 
aiin at providing a level playing field with others in the domestic and global 
market:-
(i) Reduction in the cost of credit to the extent possible with in the overall 
condition of the economy. The government should make an endeavour 
to bring it at par with other countries particularly those with whom we 
have to compete. To begin with the cost of credit could be made 
identical for both small as well as large units. 
(ii) Inducement for undertaking programmes of modernisation and 
technology up-gradation. · 
(iii) Availability of higher amounts of loan without insistence on collateral 
and third party guarantees. This will, however, depend to a great extent 
on the experience under the recently launched Credit Guarantee Fund 
Scheme. 
(iv) Creation of a widespread institutional network for credit rating for SSI 
projects at affordable cost to them.

measures adopted by the Government to strengthen the importance of this Sector in the economy 
have enabled SSis to increase their production by more than ten-fold and the employment to 
rise by over four times during the period 1973-74 to 1998-99. At the end of March, 1999, there

significant.

the limit for composite loans from Rs.5 lakhs to Rs.1 0 lakhs, raising the borrower limit for

refinance, and as at March, 2000 the list of eligible institutions for refinance consisted of 908

During the course of interaction the officials ofNABARD informed the committee that 
NABARD was set up in July, 1982 with a mandate to support through credit and other 
development efforts, agriculture, small scale industries, cottage and village industries, rural 
artisans, crafts and rural services sectors so as to promote integrated rural development. 
NABARD is essentially a development financial institution providing refinance to eligible banks 
and is not empowered to provide direct credit support. Accordingly, NABARD has introduced 
various schemes over the years for providing refinance support to Commercial Banks, State Co­
operative Banks (SCBs), State Co-operative Agriculture and Rural Development Banks

The assistance under the schemes is available to individual artisans and craftsmen, promotional 
organisations, such as government/semi government autonomous agencies, voluntary

etc. The activities eligible include Handlooms, Handicrafts, rural artisans, cottage/village, tiny

programmes of the Central/State Governments like Prime Minister' Rozgar Yojana.(PMRY},

The Committee was further informed that NABARD's refinance for investment credit 
under Non Farm Sector (excluding Government schemes) increased from Rs. 16 crore in 1986-
87 to Rs. 83 7 crore in 1999-2000 (in addition to Rs. 345 crore for SGSY amd Rs. 116 crore for 
PMRY). The cumulative refinance to eligible banks touched Rs. 4504 crore as on 31 March 
2000. This refinance has been instrumental in setting up of over 13 lakhs units and providing 
employment opportunities to around 45 lakhs persons. Within the SSI sector, NABARD's focus 
is on Tiny Sector i.e., where the investment in plant and machinery does not exceed Rs. 25 
lakhs. Refinance under Automatic Refinance Facility is available up to Rs. 15 lakhs so as to 
ensure that the client banks concentrate on smaller units. About 99% of the refinance disbursed 
so far has gone to the small units. NABARD also support good sponsored schemes like SGSY 
(ISB) and PMRY in rural areas. Short term credit limits are also sanctioned for primary weavers 
societies for procurement and marketing. 
The officials of the NABARD informed the Committee that NABARD launched District 
Rural Industries Project (DRIP) in 1993-94 on a pilot basis in 5 select districts, viz., Ganjam 
(Orissa), Kurnool (Andhra Pradesh), Gwalior (Madhya Pradesh), Sawai Madhopur (Rajasthan) 
and Sabarkantha (Gujarat) with the objective of generating sustainable employment 
opportunities on a significant scale in rural areas by providing adequate credit support together 
with promotional measures. The ground level credit for RNFS increased by about four times in 
these districts showing an average annual growth rate of 36%. 
As regards the Cluster Development, NABARD has adopted a multi-pronged strategy 
for development of clusters and other sub-sectors by conducting Product development 
workshops/Integration meets and for evolving suitable action plans covering areas such as credit 
intensification, skill development, technology development, marketing support and raw material 
supply. Consequent to the announcement of the National Programme for Rural Industrialisation 
(NPRI) in budget 1999-2000, NABARD had decided to develop 50 rural clusters on its own by 
involving other local agencies in selected districts during a 5 year period beginning from 1999-
2000. 
As regards the Gender Development, NABARD has been according special attention to 
'gender' issues in credit and support services. Conduct of training/awareness programmes, 
seminars, gender sensitization meets, formulation of exclusive schemes for women, funding 
establishment of Women Development cells in RRBs and Co-operative Banks etc., are some of 
the NABARD initiatives in this regard. 
Regarding the Promotional Initiatives, NABARD recognizes the constraints of rural 
farm and non-farm sector enterprises/entrepreneurs and the need for looking beyond credit. 
Promotion of RNFS is therefore considered as an important and necessary adjunct to its core 
refinancing function. The objective of the promotional programmes is to generate/enhance 
opportunities for employment and income in rural areas in a sustainable, demonstrative and cost

effective manner by providing grant/assistance to NGOs, Vas, Trusts and Promotional 
organisations. The assistance sanctioned for various promotional programmes by NABARD by 
31 sl March, 2000 was Rs. 35.39 crore, involving over 300 NGOs/Agencies. 
Pertaining to the Rural Entrepreneurship Development Programme (REDP), NABARD 
has been extending grant assistance to capable NGOs/Vasffraining Institutions for conducting 
REDPs for rural youth with a view to motivate and train them to set up their own small 
enterprises. So far 1958 REDPs have been sanctioned involving grant assistance ofRs. 7.38 core 
covering over 45000 trainees. NABARD adopted a comprehensive strategy to cover one lakhs 
potential entrepreneurs under REDPs over a period of 5 years (1999-2000 to 2003-2004). This 
Corporate strategy involves Institutionalisation of REDP through selection of reputed 
institutions and committing long term support to them for facilitating qualitative and quantitative 
expansion of REDPs leading to rural industrialization and economic diversification. 
With a view to strengthening the institutional capabilities of RRBs and Co-operative 
banks in addressing the gender issues in credit and support services and also to step up the flow

Maharashtra State Financial Corporation 
During the course of interaction the Committee came to know that Maharashtra State 
Financial Corporation (MSFC) was established in /\ugust 1962 under the enactment of State 
Financial Corporations Act, 1951 with the follm\ in g. ubjectives:-
(i) Function as development agency to promote and accelerate industrial growth in 
rural and backward areas of the State. 
(ii) Promote first generation entrepreneurs. 
(iii) Reduce socio-economic imbalance and create employment opportunities. 
The cumulative sanctions of the Corporation as at the end of March 2000 are Rs. 3312 
crores and cumulative disbursements of Rs.2380 crores. The share of the SSI sector in these 
cumulative sanctions works out to about 75% i.e. at around Rs.24 76.81 crores. Further, this 
assistance has created employment opportunities to about 14 lakhs persons. 
The Committee was informed that the initial developmental role played by the 
Corporation has now created certain situational weaknesses in the changed economic scenario. 
The following salient features of post-liberalisation era have largely affected financial position 
of this Corporation:-
(i) Protections like reservation of particular sector allotted to SSI were gradually 
reduced. This ultimately increased sickness and a consequential rise in NPAs of 
MSFC. . 
(ii) Liberalised import policies have suddenly affected competitiveness and 
profitability of SSis and this ultimately resulted in change from good performing 
assets to loss making assets. 
(iii) Narrowing gap between borrowing cost and lending rate of interest (i.e. spread). 
(iv) Cut throat competition from banks in term lending activity, which was initially a 
monopoly of MSFC. 
(v) Reduced financial support from State Government in terms of contribution to 
Share Capital, delay in disbursement of special Capital lncentives(SCI) and 
increase in Government guarantee fees from nil percentage to 2% per annum 
which is unprecedented in financial sector. 
In addition to the above problems, the Corporation is expected to face unequal and 
unyielding competition from other source of funds available to the entrepreneurs:-
'' I 
(i) Until now the Corporation was operating with only a single product, i.e. term 
loan to the SSI & service sector. With the amendment of SFCs Act, the scope of 
activities of the Corporation has widened. However it may take some time to 
implement it; 
(ii) Considering the present status of small scale sector on account of competition 
from the imported goods as well as adverse effect on the large and medium 
sized units on which small scale manufacturers are dependent for supply of 
components, the sickness in the small scale sector has spread at an alarming rate. 
Further, addition of the new small scale sector is also adversely affected. This 
situation has great impact on the recoveries of the Corporation consequently

OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS 
OF THE COMMITTEE 
The Committee is of the view that although Industry as a whole plays crucial role in the 
process of economic development, employment generation, equitable distribution of national 
income, mobilization of capital and entrepreneurial skills and contribution to export earnings of 
the country but SSI sector occupies an important position in the industrial economy of the 
country because of its advantages in terms of low investment, high potential for employment 
generation and wider dispersal of industries in rural and semi-urban areas. This sector offers a 
method of ensuring a more equitable distribution of national income and facilitates effective 
mobilization of resources of capital and skill which might otherwise remain unutilized. It 
further stimulates the growth of industrial entrepreneurship and promotes and diffuses the 
pattern of ownership and location. SSI sector is one. of the most vibrant and dynamic sectors of 
the Indian Economy. Over 40% of the gross turnover in manufacturing activities as also around 
35% of our exports, are contributed by SSI sector. In the area of employment generation, 
significant contribution is made by SSI sector which accounts for employment of over 1.6 crore 
workers. 
SSI sector has consistently displayed a high growth potential and employment 
generation capacity. Recognising SSI sector as a core area for growth and development of the 
Economy, the Government has from time to time taken steps to remove bottlenecks and pave the 
way for accelerating the growth of this sector by various measures, chief among them being 
streamlining the flow of Bank Credit to this sector. Public Sector Banks, on their part, have also 
made important contribution in ensuring that adequate fund flow is ensured to this sector. 
The SSI sector constitutes a major portion of the priority sector to which almost 40% of 
the bank credit is diverted. Even though no specific benchmarks are stipulated for SSI within the 
priority sector, it is ensured that out of total finance available to SSI sector 40% is granted for 
units with investment in plant and machinery. 
The Committee is happy to note that RBI has done commendable job for ensuring 
smooth credit flow to SSI sector . RBI has set up Nayak Committee in 1991 to deal with the 
aspects of adequacy and timeliness of credit to SSis and the same Committee submitted its 
report in September, 1992 with several recommendations which inter-alia include granting of 
working capital credit to SSI units computed on the basis of a minimum of 20% of their 
projected annual turnover ; giving preference to village industries, tiny industries and other 
small scale units while meeting credit requirement sector; extension of single Window 
Scheme of SIDBI to all districts; avoidance of delay in sanctioning and disbursement of 
credit to SSI sector; non-insistence on compulsory deposit as a quid-pro-quo for sanctioning 
the credit limit; opening of specialised branches; identification of sick units and urgent action 
to put them on the nursing programme; the standardized loan application forms to be used by SSI 
units; imparting of necessary training to Bank staff to handle the SSI clients. As a follow up 
of Nayak Committee recommendations , Finance Minister in the budget speech of 1995-96, 
announced seven point Action Plan for improving the flow of credit to small scale sector 
consisting of time bound action for setting up specialised SSI branches in 85 identified 
districts; at least 100 such dedicated branches to be opened before the end of 1995-96; Adequate 
delegation of powers at the branch and regional levels; Banks to conduct sample surveys of their 
performing SSI accounts to find out whether they are getting adequate credit; steps to be taken 
to see as far as possible that composite loans (covering both term loans and working capital) are 
sanctioned to SSI entrepreneurs; regular meeting by banks at zonal and regional levels with SSI 
entrepreneurs; need to sensitise bank managers and reorient them regarding working of the SSI 
51 

sector; simplification of procedural formalities by banks for SSI entrepreneurs. Accordingly, 
RBI issued instruction to banks for taking appropriate action for effective implementation of the 
seven point action plan and to keep their respective boards, apprised of the progress and also 
forward to RBI a copy of the note put up to the board. 
Concerned with the continuing problem on credit to SSI sector, RBI had set up a High 
Powered Committee in December, 1997 under the Chairmanship of Shri S.L. Kapur, Member, 
BIFR and former Secretary (SSI& ARI) to review the working of credit delivery system for 
SSis. The Committee submitted its report to RBI on 30
1
h June, 1998 and the same report contains 
126 recommendations and some of them are special treatment to smaller among small 
industries; enhancement in the quantum of composite loans; removal of procedural difficulties in 
the path of SSI advances; sorting out issues relating to mortgages of land including removal of 
stamp duty and permitting equitable mortgages; allowing access to low-cost funds to Small 
Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI) for refinancing SSI loans; Non-obtention of 
collaterals for loans up to Rs.2 lakhs; setting up of a collateral reserve fund to provide support 
to first party guarantees; setting up of a Small Industries Infrastructure Development Fund for 
developing industrial areas in around metropolitan and urban areas; change in the definition of 
sick SSI units; giving statutory powers to State Level Inter Institutional Committee (SLIIC); 
setting up of a separate guarantee organization and opening of 1,000 additional specialised 
branches; and enhancement ofSIDBI'S role and status to match with that of national Bank for 
agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD). RBI has accepted 64 recommendations of 
Kapur Committee and advised banks to implement 48 of these recommendations. During the 
course of interaction with the officials and management of various commercial banks the 
Committee was informed that the public sector banks are conforming to the recommendations 
of Nayak Committee and Kapur Committee. 
The Standing Committee on Industry, while endorsing the recommendations of the 
Nayak Committee and Kapur Committee, opines that timely and adequate credit flow to SSI 
units is the need of hour for rapid industrialization and growth of the national economy. While 
a host of issues were raised during the three days meeting at Mumbai, however, at this juncture 
the Committee while taking note of various issues to deal with at appropriate time, decided 
to dwell upon only with the credit related issues. The Committee feels that the Government 
may act promptly on following issues for continued credit flow to SSI units:-
1. MEETING OF WORKING CAPITAL REQUIREMENT 
The Committee notes the recommendations of the Nayak Committee and Kapoor 
Committee and guidelines given by RBI on the issue of the availability of working capital credit 
to SSI and the Committee is pleased to note that Government is working in right direction 
to ensure the smooth credit flow to SSI Units but at the same time the Committee is 
constraint to express in concern over the "credit gap- situation" due to non-availability of 
sufficient working capital requirement . The Committee is unhappy to note that although the· 
SSI production increased by 3.4 times but the credit availability by the banks to the units 
increased by 2.9 times only. The sordid state of affair is that despite the fact of 
recommendations made by various Committees for providing 20% of working capital 
requirement and issuance of necessary guidelines by the RBI to improve the situation in this 
regard, the availability of working capital credit has not shown any significant improvement 
and the same is bottom I ined at 7-8% . Therefore the Committee recommends that steps 
should be taken to ensure credit facilitation to SSI units upto 20% ofSSI production/turnover. 
52 

2. SUSTAIN ABLE RATE OF INTEREST 
Since the SSI units have not only to compfie with medium and Large Scale units 
but also to compete with MNCs due to ongoing liberalization and globalisation process it is 
pertinent on the part of Government to render credit facilities to SSI units at sustainable and 
oompetitive rate. The general impression of SSI associations and entrepreneurs are that 
SSI units have been exposed to phantom MNCs units without taking into account the fact of 
comparatives competitive edge and resilience which is being nurtured and nourished by 
credit facilities. During the course of interaction with SSI association the Committee came 
across that while industrial units in other countries gets credit at the rate of 4-5% per 
annum but in India SSI units is getting loan at the rate of 12 to 13% per annum. The 
Committee understands the problems of commercial banks to extend credit to SSI units at 
such a low rate of interest. Since RBI has given autonomy to Commercial Banks to decide 
their respective rate of interest the Committee feels still there is scope for lowering of rate of 
interest to some extent. The Committee not only hopes that the Commercial Banks will lend 
credit to SSI units at sustainable rate of interest but hopes strongly that Government will 
chalk out adequate measure. Incentive to induce commercial banks for extending loan at 
sustainable rate of interest. 
3. JOINT MECHANISM FOR APPRISING TERM LOANS AND WORKING 
CAPITAL 
The Committee came to know that there is no single agency for lending the term loan and 
\Vorking capital to SSI units requirement exceeding Rs 10 lakhs which leaves the SSI 
entrepreneurs to run from pillar to post. Under the circumstances, the Committee feels that 
situation may improve a lot if there is a mechanism for joint appraisal of term lending and 
working capital loan for higher amount ( about Rs.l 0 lakhs) so that there is no gap in the sanction 
of two types of loans. The measures, if undertaken, not only will save the time but also the 
money of SSI entrepreneurs, the Committee feels. 
4. WIDER ACCESS TO BANK FINANCE 
The Committee is at loss to note that only 15 to 20 percent of SSI units have access to 
Bank finance and the same findings was highlighted by a study conducted by the office of the 
DC (SSI) and Kapur Committee which caste a shadow over the credit facilities available to SSI 
Units in the country. The Committee feels that narrow access to bank finance are due to 
cumbersome procedure to access bank finance and the comprehensive conditions prescribed by 
the bank. Whatever the case may be, prevailing access to Bank finance seems to be 
narrow which must have been affecting the productivity of units engaged in SSI activities. 
Therefore, it is indispensable for credit facilitation to make adequate in conducive 
atmosphere for accessing bank finance. The Committee feels that the Government should 
undertake following measures for enabling SSI units to have access to bank finance::-
(ii) Undertaking of orientation course and adequate training for staff/officers of 
commercial banks for a change in the attitude for lending to SSI sector; 
(ii) Simplification of procedures for obtaining credit from Banks. Arrangement 
may be made for land mortgage instead of stamp duty for enabling SSI units to 
obtain credit from bank against land mortgage ; 
(iii) Government should create conducive climate for development of factoring 
services through appropriate policy prescription/legislative changes to ease 
the problems relating to stamp duty, registration for, assignment of Def'artment. 
53 

(iv) Recapitalisation and revamping of State Financial Corporation (SFCs) with the 
help ofSIDBI and lOBI enabling SFCs to lend fixed capital to SSI units; 
(v) Since Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) are most widespread with branches 
even in rural areas so well-performing RRBs may be encouraged to lend term 
loan and working capital to SSI units. 
5. POPULARISATIONOF VENTURE CAPITALFUND 
The Committee observes that assistance under venture capital fund has assumed 
importance as the liberalized regime has opened the door for a large number of 
entrepreneurs to embark upon setting up of ventures with innovative technologies and their 
commercial applications being a high-risk-high-return profile. In this regard the Committee 
would like to congratulate SlOB I for being the first financial institutions to set up a Rs.l 00 
crore National Venture Fund as a three tier strategy for development of SSis in software/IT 
industry (NFSIT) in collaboration with Ministry of Information Technology and Government 
of India. The Committee feels that the Commercial Banks should come forward in launching 
venture capital funds in all its comprehensiveness so as to effectively integrate and enhance the 
opportunities for Small Scale Industries in domestic and international market. The banks 
should endeavour to set up more and more such venture capital fund not only in software/IT 
industry but also for high growth sectors such as bio-technology and food processing. 
6. SETTING UP OF TECHNOLOGY UPGRADATION AND DEVELOPMENT 
BANKS 
The Committee observes that of obsolescence of Technology is one of the major 
problems of Small Scale Industries which has not only affected the manufacturing system and 
quality standard but also the economies of scale. Although SIDBI has come forward with 
technology development and Modernisation Fund (TDMF) Scheme in order to assist SSis at its 
prime lending rates but the Committee, taking into account the magnitude of the problem of 
technological obsolescence in SSI sector, feels that Government should come forward to set 
up Technology Upgradation and Development Banks to take stock of ground realities of 
sickness of SSI units due to obsolescence of technology and assist the units by ensuring 
credit facilitation at appropriate time and thus save the sick but potentially viable SSI units 
before dying out. 
7. EXTENSION OF NON-FINANCIAL SERVICES 
The Committee is of the view that banks have to take on a proactive role in extending 
non-financial services in the areas of technology upgradation, management training, skills 
upgradation, quality improvement, environment management, information about markets, 
regulations and clients, etc. Commercial banks and SFCs can study the package of non-financial 
services offered by the Business Development Bank of Canada (BDC), SIDBI etc., and adopt 
them with such modifications as are considered appropriate. The Committee is of the view that a 
loan application should be given along with "Small Business Growth Kit" with a guide to prepare 
business plans and a series of financial ratio calculators followed by a free consulting session of 
personalized solutions to meet the needs of small and medium sized business at every stage in 
their development including export solutions and quality solutions. Moreover, banks should come 
forward for finding foreign buyers by identifying possible export markets, undertaking market 
research projects, identifying the barriers to entry and to promote products to trade fairs and 
foreign missions. Financial Institution should also facilitate the product for the foreign market and 
outlining the national logistics such as transportation, shipping, insurance and documentation and 
developing the network of physical distribution of the product besides arranging to provide the 
legal and accounting service in the target market. Not only this, financial institution should also 
54 

provide assistance to small scale entrepreneurs in risk management by obtaining credit 
information on foreign buyers. helping insurance against commercial and political risk of non­
payment. helping finance foreign receivable and providing assistance when the small business has 
to issue a bond or a performance guarantee. That is to say, banks need to play the role of a friend, 
philosopher and guide to their SSI clients. 
8. PRIME MINISTER'S ANNOUNCEMENT OF PACKAGE FOR SSI SECTOR 
The Committee observes that the Government is really serious about removing the 
problem . specially credit related, of SSI Sector . The Committee feels that the Composite 
Loans Scheme wherein the loan limit has been raised from Rs.l 0 lakh to Rs.25 lakhs will go a 
long way in meeting the credit requirements of tiny units through single financing agency. 
Similarly, the enhancement in investment limit. of industry related services and business 
enterprises from Rs.S lakhs to Rs.l 0 lakhs will enable large number of enterprises to have 
access to priority sector credit. Moreover the Committee is happy to note that the Government 
is taking required steps for technology upgradation and therefore announced a Capital subsidy 
of 12% for investment in technology upgradation. Presently, the Government has given the 
capital subsidy in select sectors. The Committee feels that the Ministry of SSI and A&RI 
should examine whether such capital subsidy is required in other sectors of SSI for technology 
upgradation and if so, the Ministry should take up the issue at the appropriate level. The 
Committee is happy to observe the enhancement of project limit under National Equity Fund 
of SIDBI from Rs. 25 lakhs to Rs.SO lakhs which will further help the tiny sector because 30% 
of investment under NEF Scheme has been bracketed for tiny sector . The Committee is 
also pleased to observe the announcement of Credit Guarantee Fund Scheme, operated by 
Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Small Industries (GIS!) jointly set up by the Government of 
India and SIDBI, with the corpus of Rs.125 crore (contributed Rs.l 00 crores by 
Government of India and Rs.25 crores by SIDBI) and hopes that SSI units will have access to 
bank credit without collateral fee and third party guarantee. 
The Committee would like to extend its congratulation to SIDBI & NSIC for their 
continuance to give concessional rate of refinance/finance to tiny sectors. The Committee 
feels that Government would take urgent steps to revitalize/restructure State Finance 
Corporation enabling them to lend term loan to SSI units. The Committee also hopes that RBI 
would take concrete steps to strengthen and popularize factoring services to encourage bill 
culture in order to remove the problems of delayed payment ofSSI units. Once the problem of 
delayed payment is solved SSI units would be in a better position to recycle their profit into 
capital and in a way solve the problem • of working capital, the Committee feels . The 
Committee further observes that since sickness of SSI units is a chronic problem, a serious 
thought and timely action is required for rehabilitation of currently sick but potentially viable 
SSI units . The Committee hopes that RBI will be successful in its current efforts to draw a 
detailed , transparent and non-discretionary guidelines and same will be issued for effective 
implementation before the sick but potentially viable SSI units go beyond the point of no 
return. 
The Committee appreciates the steps taken by the Government and feels that 
policy/package which have been envisaged/extending to SSI sector will not suffer the problem 
of implementation gap. While appreciating the steps taken by the Government to ensure the 
smooth credit flow to SSI sector, the Committee hopes that all the policy and programme 
will see the light of the day and the Government and its machinery should be equally 
enthusiastic in implementing the package . In this regard the Committee recommends that 
the Ministry of SSI and A&RI while furnishing the Action Taken Note on the 
recommendations contained in the present Report will give detailed note with regard to 
55 

Action taken and its impact of each and every scheme under the present package for SSI 
units. 
9. SHRIMAHILAGRIHUDYOG LIJJAT PAPAD 
The Committee is highly impressed with the activities of Shri Mahila Udyog Lijjat 
Papad - a cooperative society which is engaged in various activities thereby not only giving 
employment to 40 thousand women workers but also serving the society in more than one 
way. The Committee feels that this model organisation should act as catalyst for further 
proliferation of such non-government organisations. The Committee feels that the 
Government should come forward and encourage such organisations and the banks and 
financial institution should extend the requisite credit. The Government should also help such 
organisation by extending tax concessions. 
I 0. KHADI AND VILLAGE INDUSTRIES COMMISSION (KVIC) 
While appreciating the role of KVIC in general the Committee feels that the KVIC 
should play more active role for promotion. and encouragement of Khadi and Village 
Industries:-
\ ''(f~-~ 
(i) The Ministry of SSI &Jd A&RI in tandem with KVIC should take up the 
issue of seeking cou'Qter gua~antee with the Governments of Assam and Bihar 
so that subsidy may b'e·provided by the KVIC to these States for the general 
benefit of the people; \ 
(ii) The Committee is of the view that the Government should allocate maximum 
budgetary support to th~ ~ec,tor of SSI which have the maximum potential 
for employment generation ; · · 
(iii) The Committee while expressing serious concern over accumulation of 
inventory to the tune of Rs.750 crore recommends that KVIC should take an 
all out efforts for clearing all the inventory in the minimum possible time . 
KVIC should sketch effective marketing strategy for clearing the stocks which 
has piled up over the years.; and 
(iv) The Committee feels that KVIC should also enhance the R&D efforts for 
better designing and quality of Khadi products and undertake measures for 
popularization of Khadi products on the lines of the slogan " Use Khadi 
products and be a proud Indian" . 
The Committee hopes that in the light of the observations and recommendations in this 
Report the Ministry of Small Scale Industries and Agro & Rural Industries should activate 
itself to meet the challenges ahead of it which has emerged due to on going liberalisation 
and globalisation processes and feel encouraged to approach the Ministry of Finance for 
ensured credit flow to small scale industries.

OBSERVATIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS
 
 
            As is evident from the subject of study assigned to the Sub-Committee, it was required to review the
performance of Central Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) under the administrative domain of the Department of
Heavy Industry, Ministry of Heavy Industries  and Public Enterprises.  Accordingly,  the Sub-Committee embarked
upon the most talked issue, namely, the performance of the Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs)  in the changed scenario
of the Indian economy.  The Sub-Committee, while having interaction with the Workers and Management of select 6
subsidiary companies  of the Holding Company, i.e.,  Bharat Yantra Nigam Ltd. (BYNL), had an opportunity to analyse
the factors responsible for the present state of decline of some of these PSUs.  These PSUs, for long, had lived under a
protective regime and the opening up of the economy had meant opening of floodgates of unforeseen  problems for
some of them.  Transmission from a closed economy to a free economy has caught them and exposed their
vulnerability.  There is a host of reasons which culminated into present crisis.  State protection can no longer be there to
shield them against the onslaught unleashed by  their rivals in the present competitive and consumer-oriented market.  
It is apparent that the present crisis in some of these PSUs  is a simple case of gross managerial inefficiency and sheer
lack of  foresightedness on the part of those who have been at the helm of affairs. 
 
The first major problem, which warrants the attention of this Sub-Committee, is the delay in approval of the
restructuring of the subsidiary companies of BYNL .  It is felt that Department of Industry, Ministry of Heavy
Industries  and Public Enterprises seems to have a very indifferent approach towards the preparation, approval and
implementation of the restructuring packages for these subsidiary companies.
 
The Sub-Committee feels that any delay on the whole process involving the restructuring of a Company smacks
of lack of commitment  on the part of the Government.  Therefore, the Sub-Committee recommends that the Department
of Heavy Industry , Ministry of Heavy Industries  and Public Enterprises, should make conscious  efforts to help these
subsidiary companies by approval , timely preparation, and implementation of their restructuring- packages.

            The issue of  timely payment of arrears and strategy to reduce  the employees of these subsidiary companies
merit the Sub-Committee’s serious consideration as it has a direct bearing on the well-being of thousands of employees.
For years together, there has been no wage revision in some of these  PSUs as a result of which the moral of the
employees has touched its  nadir.  Some of these PSUs have  also defaulted in the payment of  statutory dues  like
gratuity, PF, etc. of the employees because of shortage of funds.  The argument advanced by the Government  for non-
payment of wage etc. was that the responsibility of payment to employees lies with the  companies  themselves and the
issue is being examined by a Group of Ministers. 
 
            The whole issue is a sensitive one and it affects the employees in various ways.  The Sub-Committee, therefore,
recommends that arrears and statutory  dues  should be paid  to the employees forthwith by earmarking separate funds
for this purpose .  The Ministry merely becoming a helpless spectator  in the matter  by saying that the matter is being
examined by a Group of Ministers does not end the responsibility of the Administrative Ministry. The Ministry  should
own the responsibility in this regard and take up  the matter  seriously with the Government at appropriate forum for the
release of  funds for the payments of wage arrears, statutory dues, etc. by arranging some separate fund for the purpose,
if necessary,  in conjunction with other Ministries  whose  PSUs are also not able to pay  salaries to their employees.
During the visit of the Committee to various subsidiaries companies it was found that there was not enough work
order with these subsidiaries as a result of  which  the entire  activities of  these subsidiary companies may come to a
grinding halt at any moment.
 
            The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department of Heavy Industry, Ministry of Heavy Industries
and Public Enterprises, should   take up the matter with the Union Cabinet and necessary instructions should be  issued
for those customer-PSUs and Departments for placing adequate orders on these  subsidiaries of  BYNL.
 
 Many subsidiaries are having excess manpower that has proved a handicap to function in the post liberalization
era . Although planned rationalization of manpower by offering attractive packages   could solve the problem,  the flow
of funds for the implementation of  Voluntary Retirement Schemes  (VRS)  still remains far below the required mark. 
The Sub-Committee, therefore, recommends that  wherever the  planed VRS can facilitate a firm ground , the
Government should make requisite financial support available to that particular  PSU  without delay.
 
 During the interaction with the Officials of the customer PSUs/ concerned Departments of these  PSUs the Sub-
Committee was informed that the delivery record of these PSUs is very poor. The Sub-Committee, therefore, 
recommends the need for timely execution of orders / projects in order to avoid subsequent delay in completion of the
projects of the customer PSUs / Departments as it ,in turn, helps them to avoid cost and time over-runs.  The Sub-
Committee, therefore, recommends that all PSUs should evolve a proper workable mechanism to meet the deadline for
supply of orders.  The Sub-Committee further recommends that in case the delivery is before the deadline, there should
be some provision for rewarding the supplier PSU in some form.
 
Through the interaction with various PSUs it also came to the notice of the Sub-Committee that fair amount of
money of various PSUs is locked-up with the State Government Agencies like State Electricity Board, Power houses,
State Irrigation Department, State PSUs, etc.  As a result the Company is not able to make payments to their suppliers
and it is also not in a position to pay  monthly wages to their employees.  The Sub-Committee is perplexed to see such a
helpless situation.  The Sub-Committee , therefore, recommends that the Department of Heavy Industry should take up
the matter with the State Governments for release of such dues .Otherwise, in the alternative , they should take up the
matter with the Planning Commission and inform them the details of dues yet to be released by the State Government
agencies and to impress upon the Planning Commission to consider this aspect before  allocation of funds to the State
Governments.       It has also come to the notice of the Sub-Committee that earlier these PSUs were getting orders from
the State Government Agencies but now the State Governments have started  placing their orders with their own PSUs
or any other private agencies for its requirements. The Sub-Committee feels that like the Central PSUs which are giving
some purchase preference to the Central PSUs, the State Government may also be requested to give some purchase
preference to the Central PSUs and the Central PSUs may also give  some purchase  preference to the State PSUs.  The
placement of work-orders   by State PSUs  to Central PSUs  and vice-versa will take Government PSUs  a long way in 
post  liberalization period  which will  usher in a  new chapter in the   relationship between the Central and State
Governments.

The Committee also came to know  during its  interaction  with the  workers and  Management of  some PSUs 
that due to  non-delivery of  final goods  in scheduled time,  penalties   have been  imposed  on  them  in  the  form  of
Liquidity  Damages (LD)  which are proving  a death knell  for some of  them.
 
The Department of Heavy Industry should take up the matter with the client PSUs for release of outstanding
amount locked-up on  account   of Liquidity  Damages (LD)  to such a possible extent which can be  released by the
client PSUs. This will be a helpful gesture to the PSUs who are having working capital
problem.                                                
 
The Sub-Committee would now like to address itself to the specific problems of these PSUs and make suitable
observations and recommendations accordingly.
 
 
BRIDGE AND ROOF COMPANY(INDIA) LTD.
 
1.         The capital-restructuring proposal of Bridge and Roof Company  has been pending since 1991. The Capital
restructuring proposals of Rs.42.57 crores  has already been submitted to the Government.  However,  proposal  has not
been approved   by the Government   till date.  This inexplicable delay in the approval of the proposal is coming in the
way of the companies’ efforts to borrow from the open market to meet the total capital requirement. 
The Sub-Committee has taken a serious note of this undue delay and recommend that capital restructuring of the
Company should be approved by the Government at the earliest.
  2.       Bridge and Roof Company  was  awarded  a contract for `Design, engineering, supply, installation and
commissioning of storage facility at four locations,viz., Thankot, Amlekhgunj, Kathmandu and Pokhara in Nepal, by
Nepal Oil Corporation Limited (A Nepal Government Undertaking) valued at Rs. 17.77  cores in March, 1994. Out of
four sites works at three sites have been completed and Fuel has been stored in all the Tanks.  The work was
accomplished despite a lot of constraints and delay faced by Bridge and Roof Company  due to reasons beyond the
Company’s control . Fourth terminal at Pokhara has been abandoned/foreclosed by NOC on their  own due to local
villagers’ problem/land  dispute.
 
            Since commissioning of the storage facilities built by B&R NOC has been using  three  terminals for storage of
Fuel and other purposes, formally taken over the sites and issuing  substantial completion certificate as  per the  contract
condition.  They have also not  taken-over the fourth terminal at Pokhara though they have foreclosed the same. NOC
are not paying dues of approximately Rs.12.90 crores comprising schedule bills, extra work bills, escalation bills and
claim.
 
            Due to above situation, B&R’s Bank-Guarantees towards (a) Mobilisation Advance ((Rs.2.69 crores) and (b)
Performance Guarantee (Rs.3.54 crores) are blocked. As a result this, Bank-Guarantees have to  be extended a number
of times draining Rs.30 lakhs annually due to bank charges only. Consequently, Bridge and Roof Company  has to
perforce maintain the establishment at Nepal since they can not abandon the project unless the terminals are formally
taken over by NOC.  This involves  recurring expenditure around Rs.6 lakhs per month.  If Bridge and Roof Company 
do not continue to extend the   Bank-Guarantees  as demanded by NOC or decide to leave the project now, NOC is
likely  to encash  Bank-Guarantees and foreclosed  outstanding- payments.
The Sub-Committee, therefore, recommends that Department of Heavy Industry should used the Good Offices
of the Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of External Affairs to help release of payments by Nepal Oil Corporation to
Bridge & Roof Company.     
 
 
BHARAT HEAVY PLATES AND VESSELS LIMITED.
 
3.         Bharat Heavy Plates and Vessels has been confronting with the problems of  shortage of working  capital and
non-payment of salaries on time which has affected  the smooth functioning of the Company.  It requires  the financial

support from the Government to help out  the Company of these two  problems. 
 
The Sub-Committee , therefore, recommends that immediate steps  for filling the gap of working capital should
be taken by the Government.
 
4.         Apart from the allocation of a sum of Rs.10.00 crores under plan budget for 2000-2001, issuance of counter
guarantee with 50% interest subsidy is already under consideration of the Government so as to enable the Company to
raise  Rs.15 crores through the  issues of bonds  for implementation of Voluntary Retirement Scheme (VRS).
The Sub-Committee, therefore,  recommends a immediate acceptance of the Demand of counter guarantee with
budgetary support pending before the Government.
 
5.         Bharat Heavy Plates and Vessels  has been suffering from  severe liquidity crunch and consequent upon the 
recovery of Liquidity Damages (LDs) by  the client PSUs the Company is facing the cash-flow  related problems.  It
requires a financial support  from the Government to correct the financial imbalances  in the Company.
 
The Sub-Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department of Heavy Industry should take the matter with
customer PSUs/Department for releasing of Liquidity Damages (LDs)  so that the shortage of working capital can be
met from the released  fund .
 
 
RICHARDSON & CRUDDAS LIMITED.
 
6.         Richardson & Cruddas Ltd. is  one of the PSUs which has been functioning successfully after the 
implementation of  revival package but  still the Company is facing a major  problem  of excess manpower . Secondly
due to the excess manpower they has been no wage   revision of the employees  for long as a result of which the moral
of the employees has touched its  nadir. 
 
 The Sub-Committee, therefore, recommends immediate sanction of  requisite funds for  the implementation of
Voluntary Retirement Scheme (VRS)  and wage-revision of the employee as any delay would not be  in the interest of
the Company.
 
7.         One of the units of the Company,  i.e.,  the Byculla Unit, has been making  losses.  Secondly, the excess
manpower  has been  eating   the substantial  funds of the Company. Though, this Company is a marginally profit
making Company, yet it is   being denied the central financial assistance in the form of grant under VRS head. The
Government should look into this problem from a different angle. If the Company is allotted the required funds for VRS
the excess manpower of the Byculla Unit can be down-sized and the Unit can be put back on right track.
            The Sub-Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should sympathetically consider the grants for
VRS to save the Byculla Unit.
 
8.         With the  advent of  private sector the customer PSUs/Departments  have started placing their work-orders on
other private companies which were earlier  being placed on Richardsons  & Cruddas Ltd.  One of its units, Byculla
unit, has not been receiving any work-orders for its products from Railways, an old customer of the Company.
 
The Sub-Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department of Heavy Industry should initiate  the matter
with the Ministry of Railways and do needful for placing  the work-orders  on Richardsons & Cruddas Ltd. 
 
 
TUNGABHADRA STEEL PRODUCTS LTD.
 
9.         Due to non-availability of work-orders and delay in the realization of the payments of the outstanding dues, the
Company has been passing through a severe financial crunch. The Company has also requested for the implementation
of financial-restructuring. Under its proposed  financial restructuring   proposal the Company has  required  that the
Bank guarantee should be replaced by Indemnity Bonds for obtaining advance payments.
