The Sub-Committee therefore,  recommends that Government should take steps to implement the financial
restructuring of the Company.
 
10.       Tungabhadra Steel Products Ltd.  has not paid  the statutory dues   like PF. ST, ESIC, CISF dues, etc.  The
Company requires grant  from the Government to pay of  these outstanding  dues.
The Sub-Committee,  therefore, recommends that the Ministry should explore the possibility to give some
financial assistance to the Company so as  to enable it  to pay of these  above statutory dues. 
 
11.       In the present  economic scenario   there is an  acute shortage of  work-orders and  Company has been unable
procure  orders   even after  assurance   by the State Governments  and Central PSUs.
 
            The Sub-Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry should taken the matter with the Central PSUs  as
well as State PSUs for adequate work-orders for the Company.
 
 
BHARAT PUMPS AND COMPRESSORS LIMITED
12.       Bharat Pumps and Compressors needs immediate financial- restructuring  as recommended by SBI Capital
Markets so as to enable the  Company  to  pay-off   its loans  and interests pending for long and facilitate  the 
Company   to  enter  into  Joint-Ventures.  It will enable the Company to face  the  challenges  in the aftermath of 
emergence of  liberalisation and globalisation  in  the present  Indian economic scenario.
 
The Sub-Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department of Heavy Industry should  examine  the
financial restructuring  of the company as    prepared by ICICI and  approved by BIFR . 
 
13.       Bharat Pumps and Compressors is already under a financial burden of  Government loans and interests and
pending  for long . Keeping under  consideration the poor financial  status of the Company it is required that these loans
and interests  may be deferred.
 
The Sub-Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government’s  loans and interests   amounting  to Rs.20.32 
crores  should be deferred  and repayment should   start from  2003-2004.
 
14.       In the stiff  competition posed by domestic  and overseas suppliers  Bharat Pumps and Compressors has been
facing  challenges  from the private sector  due to which work-orders have been declining.    Further, the customers  
have started    opting for  Lumpsum Turnkey (LSTK) projects for contract  exhibition and also imposing stiff  terms and
conditions   which the company is unable to meet  due to  obsolete plant & machinery and shortage of working capital.
 
The Sub-Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government   should initiate action to  secure  orders from
the Central PSUs of the Oil and other Core Sector on nomination  basis at competitive prices and terms and conditions .
Funds should be granted to the Company to meet the working capital requirement and install more sophisticated 
machines to upgrade quality of products for final delivery of the products.
 
 
 TRIVENI STRUCTURALS  LTD.
15.       Triveni Structurals  Ltd. has been facing a critical  financial crisis    due to  which    it has not   paid    
outstanding/statutory  dues.    There    is   a  requirement    for    the      approval     a rehabilitation package  as per the
recommendations  of  CRISIL.
 
            The Sub-Committee , therefore, recommends that a revised  rehabilitation package  should be sanctioned by the
Department of Heavy Industry and necessary funds  should be released   for meeting  the outstanding statutory dues,
working capital , VRS , Salary, etc.

16.       There is an acute  shortage of working capital in the TSL  which has been hampering  the smooth functioning of
the Company.  This has resulted  in  delaying  the   projects  which requires   an  immediate sanction of short-term 
loans  for  meeting the working -capital requirement.
 
            The Sub-Committee, therefore, recommends  that the Government should find out ways and means for
generating the working  capital for  the Company.
 
 
BHARAT YANTRA NIGAM LIMITED (BYNL)
 
            The Committee observed that BYNL as a holding company has not been able to assist its subsidiaries to come
out of the wood. The Committee, therefore, recommends that all the six subsidiaries of the BYNL should be merged
into a single Company  so that the newly merged Company can pool together all the resources of the subsidiaries and
stand on a sound economic ground and this may help them in bidding for LSTK projects and by having effective control
on its Units act as the main agent for  securing  orders, rationalizing manpower, ensuring VRS grant from the 
Government, etc. and eventually emerge as a pioneer to the other Central /State  PSUs.

CHAPTER – I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS ACCEPTED BY THE  GOVERNMENT
 
 
3.
 
RECOMMENDATION
 
                        Closely linked with it is the disturbing fact of which the Sub-Committee has taken a serious note,
is the inexplicable dithering on the part of the Department of Heavy Industry when it comes to supporting the
revival package of a sick company. The Sub-Committee came across a number of cases wherein the Department
backed out at the eleventh hour in the proceedings of the BIFR by expressing its inability to support the revival
plan of a PSU referred to the BIFR.  This ambivalence in the approach of the    Department leads the Sub-
Committee to conclude that  it has acted like a fair weather friend with an ulterior motive to ultimately wash its
hands off those PSUs who are  in the moribund state.
               The Sub-Committee, therefore, recommends to the Department of  Heavy  Industry  to  take the revival
packages of the sick PSUs to their logical  conclusion  by  assuring  the  BIFR  of providing full financial
backing to any such revival plan.
 
COMMENTS
 
               Govt. is committed to the revival of sick PSUs, if a credible and viable revival plan emerges. 27 sick
PSEs under DHI have been referred to BIFR. Rehabilitation schemes have     been sanctioned by BIFR in the
case of 12 PSEs which are under implementation for which Govt. have provided fresh infusion of funds to the
extent of Rs.637 crores and financial restructuring of Rs.2063 crores. No time is lost in release of funds and
issue of necessary sanctions for conversion of loans into equity etc. once a BIFR revival package is sanctioned.
 
FURTHER COMMENTS
 
         A list indicating the name of PSUs and their date of reference to BIFR is given at Annexure-I.
 
         In the case of 8 PSUs, the revival plans are awaiting recommendations of BIFR.  Govt. has been
extending financial assistance for meeting working capital requirements including  payment of salary and wages
and for Voluntary Retirement Scheme (VRS)  to these PSUs besides funds for investments under plan..  Details
of  assistance provided by the Govt. during  the years 1998-99, 1999-2000 & 2000-01 (upto 31.1.2001) in case
of these 8 PSUs, and their  present status are given at Annexure - II.
 
4.
RECOMMENDATION
 
               The  issue of non-payment of arrears and statutory dues of the  employees  of  these  PSUs  merits  this 
Sub-Committee's serious  consideration  as  it  has  a  direct  bearing on the well-being of thousands of
employees.  For  years  altogether, there has  been  no wage revision in some of these PSUs.  As a result, the
morale of the employees has touched its nadir with a clear reflection on their productivity and motivation. This
apart, a majority of these PSUs have  also  defaulted  in  the payment  of statutory dues like gratuity, provident
fund, etc. of the employees.  In some cases where the wage  revision  has been  effected, employees have not
been paid arrears for long.                
               The whole issue is a sensitive one as it affects the employees in different  ways.    Hence,  the  Sub-
Committee  has taken a sympathetic note of it. Accordingly, the Sub-Committee recommends that arrears and
statutory dues of the employees should be  paid  forthwith  by earmarking separate  funds  for the purpose.  A

45th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/45threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:12:22]
step like this would not only raise the motivational level of  the  employees but  also improve the industrial
relations to the advantage of these PSUs.
 
COMMENTS
 
               A Group of Ministers was constituted by the Govt. to work out a strategy for liquidation of statutory
dues owed to workers employed in Central PSEs. It was recommended by the members of the GOM in its
meeting held on 10.4.2000 to work out a PSU-wise strategy for liquidation of workers dues according to the
following three categories (i) PSUs which need  to be closed down after exploring all possibilities of revival; (ii)
PSUs that can be revived through restructuring and (iii) PSUs that are operating and can meet statutory dues of
workers from internal resources.
 
               Strategies for liquidation of statutory dues in respect of PSUs under DHI are as under :-
                                i.      In the case of sick units where revival plans have been sanctioned, the statutory dues are being
liquidated as per the recommendations and the time frame indicated in the revival plan. These PSUs
are Braithwaite, BPCL, Jessop, BSCL, BBVL, RBL, R&C, TSL, HEC, ILK, SIL and NIL.
                              ii.      There are other loss-making PSUs for which revival plans are under formulation. Liabilities on
account of statutory dues are being considered in their revival packages. These are HMT, TCIL,
NEPA & HPF.
                             iii.      In respect of unviable sick PSUs, Govt. has decided clear the statutory dues alongwith benefits
under voluntary Separation Scheme (VSS).
 
 
FURTHER COMMENTS
 
               35 out of 48 PSUs under the Deptt. had outstanding statutory dues of Rs. 562 Crs.  As  on 30.9.2000.  
PSU-wise/category-wise  details  are  given  in the Annexure III. 
Strategies for liquidation of these statutory dues are :
 
(i)     PSUs facing winding up/closure      
Provision has  been made in the budget for liquidating statutory dues of Rs.        63 cr. to PSUs facing
winding up / closure  under Voluntary Separation Scheme (VSS) which was introduced in these PSUs
in September, 2000.  The dues are being cleared in phases to the employees availing VSS.
 
       (ii)      PSUs having revival plan sanctioned by BIFR.  
Out of the 12 PSUs having revival plan sanctioned by BIFR, 3 PSUs  namely Burn Standard Co. Ltd.
(BSCL), National Instruments Ltd. (NIL) and Braithwaite and Co. are expected to clear their statutory
dues out of their own internal generation.  The cases of remaining PSUs will be considered on merits
for providing financial support out of the budgetary provision of Rs. 150 cr. made in RE 2000-2001
and Rs. 150 cr. in BE 2001-2002.
 
(iii)      PSUs awaiting sanction of revival plans                    
7 PSUs falling in this category have statutory dues of Rs. 104 cr. as on       30.9.2000.  The dues of
these PSUs will be included in the revival plans and also be considered for liquidation out of the
budgetary provision made for the purpose referred in para above.
 
(iv)      Other   loss Making PSUs.
Statutory dues of HMT and HCL, whose restructuring plan have been recently approved by the Govt.,
are envisaged to be cleared out of their internal resources.  The proposals for liquidating dues of the
remaining 3 loss making PSUs shall be included in their plans for revival/JV formation.
 
 (v)       Profit making PSUs
The total statutory dues of Rs. 11.10 cr. are envisaged to be cleared out of internal resources in respect
of 4 profit-making PSUs.

5.
RECOMMENDATION
 
              As described elsewhere in this Report, these  PSUs  have  long been nurtured  in the shadow of state
protectionism.  With the change in the overall industrial economic scenario, they  have become the  victims  of
circumstances.  There was a time, when they did not have to toil hard to  get  work  orders  to  keep their
workshops running as they were assured of regular orders from their  customer  PSUs/Departments.   Things  
are no  longer   the   same  as   they  once  used to be.  Hence, the present critical order book position. Now,
these PSUs are not only facing stiff  challenge  from the  indigenous  private  sector  companies  but also from
the multinationals.    The   change-over   from   the   days    of `no-competition' to an era of `fierce competition'
is the bane of all the woes of these PSUs. That is why, this Sub-Committee strongly feels that these PSUs
deserve a  thoughtful  consideration.  Any attempt to downplay their importance could  have  serious 
ramifications  for  all concerned.   In  the  opinion of the Sub-Committee, these PSUs should be given enough 
elbow  room  to  adapt  themselves  in accordance with  the  new realities.  For this, they need some degree of
protection by way of reserving a fixed percentage of work orders of the  customer  PSUs/Departments  for  at 
least another  four  to  five  years  so  that they are able to grow enough teeth to take on their rivals.
 
               Therefore,   the   Sub-Committee   recommends   that   the Department  of  Heavy  Industry  should 
prepare  a   detailed PSU-wise  note  giving  each  company's order book requirement from the customer PSUs
and the Departments of the  Government. Any  such  note,  then  be placed before the Union Cabinet for  
having   necessary instructions issued for  all  those  customer  PSUs and Departments for placing adequate
orders on these PSUs of the  Department of Heavy Industry.  The Sub-Committee hopes that Department of

RECOMMENDATION
 
               During the course of its study, the Sub-Committee had a close look at the managerial aspect of these
PSUs and the need for granting functional  autonomy  to  them.  It was informed that lack of  professionalism 
amongst  the  Management  is  mainly responsible for  the  sickness  of  these  companies.    Inept handling of
the affairs has brought these PSUs to such a pass. Lack of functional  autonomy  also  aggravated  the  state  of
affairs. Therefore,  in  the  opinion of  the Sub-Committee, the need of the hour is to appoint full-time and
seasoned professionals to run the affairs of these companies and  give  them  greater functional  autonomy  to
enable them to deal with new emerging challenges with boldness and in a professional manner. At the same
time, Government should also find out, apart from the extraneous reasons, the administrative and managerial
failure in respect of these PSUs and fix accountability and responsibility.
 
 
COMMENTS
 
               Govt. has been giving more and more functional autonomy to PSUs to enable them work on
commercial lines and improve their viability. In the past 696 Govt. guidelines which were applicable for Central
PSUs have been scrapped. Greater autonomy is being given for MOU signing companies. Some of the
companies have been identified as Navratnas  (BHEL) and Mini-ratnas (HNL, HMT (I) and REIL) which entitle
them to additional autonomy in the area of investments, personnel policies, raising capital from domestic and
international markets and entering into joint ventures etc. So far as accountability is concerned, the Chief
Executives are being appraised with reference to objective parameters of performance and efficiency that takes
into account achievements of various targets, control over the organization etc.
 
 
FURTHER COMMENTS
 
               During the last three years no additional autonomy has been given to the MOU signing companies in
the area of capital investments, personnel policies, raising capital from domestic and international market and
entering into joint venture, etc.

RECOMMENDATION
 
               Rationalisation of  excessive  manpower  is  another  area  of concern for these PSUs.  As stated earlier,
one of the motives behind  these  companies,  being  in the public sector as they are,  was  to   generate  
adequate   number   of   employment opportunities   for  the  growing  populace  of  the  country. Accordingly, it
was in  the  fitness  of  things  to  adopt  a liberal recruitment  policy.   However, the negative result of  this
liberal policy began to be felt with the onset of economic liberalisation which caused depletion of  profit as it
was now beyond the reach of these PSUs to sustain their large workforce.  In case of a number of these PSUs,
the presence of excessive manpower is proving  to  be  a major  stumbling  block  in their attempt to regain their

Government should make requisite financial support available to that  PSU  without  any  delay.  Because

Of these problems, one major problem whose tentacles are spread over just about every PSU, is the loans
given to them by the Government.  Conversion of these loans into equity would not only  reduce  the  burden of
debt and the interest  accrued on it but would also enable these beleaguered PSUs  to embark on  a  major 
financial  restructuring.  Besides, these companies will be in a position to get commercial borrowings to meet
their immediate requirement for working capital. It  is,   therefore,   the   considered   view   of  this Sub-
Committee that the Department  of  Heavy  Industry  should prepare a comprehensive  financial restructuring
package for all these PSUs so that they  are  able  to  bounce  back  with vigour and  vitality.  This package
should also address itself to the interest accrued on the loans, as  mere  conversion  of loan into equity would not
serve any meaningful purpose in the absence of waiver of interest.
 
 
COMMENTS

funds, Govt. guarantees apart from conversion of loan into equity/debenture. These proposals are formulated and
approved after careful consideration by various agencies. Amongst the BIFR referred companies, revival plans
have been sanctioned by BIFR in case of 12 PSUs. In these cases write off of interest/loan is to Rs.1616 crs. And
conversion of loan into equity/debenture amounts to Rs.447 cr. In addition revival plans include fresh infusion of
funds of Rs.637 crs. and Govt. guarantees for Rs.625 crs. Details are attached at Annexure-VII.

RECOMMENDATION
 
                        During its interaction with the officials  of  customer  PSUs/ Departments of these PSUs, the Sub-

RECOMMENDATIONS
 
             Hindustan Photo  Films Manufacturing Company Ltd.  is the only company  in  the  country   engaged  
in   the   photo   films manufacturing   and  is  one  of  the  world's  six  photo film manufacturers.   Before 
liberalisation,  it   enjoyed   total monopoly, but with the onset of liberalisation it began to lose its  grip  over 
the  market   because   of   the availability  of imported cheap photo goods of multinationals in  the  country.
Presently,  the  company  is in dire straits and struggling to weather the vagaries of liberalisation.  For a reversal
in its fortunes, the company needs a major financial restructuring. In the opinion of the Sub-Committee, the
Government should provide  requisite  support for financial restructuring of the company in order to enable it to 
come  out  of  the  trap  of sickness.
 
             The interests of Hindustan Photo Films  Manufacturing  Company Limited are being hit hard by the
existing duty structure. Although,  the customs duty on the polyester sub-base which is used for manufacturing
films by HPF  Ltd.,  has  been  brought down  to  nil, there is need for enhancing customs duty on the imported
semi-finished and finished photo goods. Therefore,  the  Sub-Committee recommends a steep increase in the
customs duty levied on the import of semi-finished  and finished photo goods to protect HPF Ltd.
 
 
COMMENTS
 
               HPF was referred to BIFR on 14.10.95 and was declared sick on 23.01.96. Revival of the Company is
under consideration of GOI/BIFR. Based on the reports of OA (IDBI), Consultant (PWC)  & the management of
HPF, a draft note for the Cabinet seeking financial and fiscal relieves to HPF is under finalisation.
 
               The Deptt. of Heavy Industry have been requesting Ministry of Finance, Deptt. of Revenue to increase
customs duty on import of semi-finished and finished photo goods to protect the interests of HPF and to allow it
a level playing field. This is again proposed to be included in the proposed draft note for the Cabinet to revive
HPF, as one of the incentives to be provided to HPF.
 
 
FURTHER COMMENTS
 
A Note for the Cabinet has been submitted to the Cabinet Sectt. on 10.1.2001 to revive the company
through support and financial restructuring.

RECOMMENDATION
 
               One such company which has successfully withstood the changes brought about by the liberalisation of
Indian economy. The impressive track record of it calls for a special mention of its achievements. As a matter of
fact, BHEL is a role model for other PSUs of Ministry of Heavy Industry. For, it has managed to stay in the race
despite the odds faced by it as a result of stiff competition unleashed by the multinational giants operating in its
field of  specialisation namely, manufacture of power plants. Though, BHEL has managed to sustain its viability
yet it is facing some unfair challenges. The absence of a level playing field vis-à-vis its multinational
competitors has been posing stiff challenges to the company. This is leading to an ever increasing pressure on
the profitability of  it. Despite this, the company has been constantly upgrading its technology and has also been
successful in acquiring state of the art technology used in HVDC power projects. This reflects the commitment
of the company as a whole to serve the nation even when the odds are stacked against it. Therefore, what this
company requires is little help from the Government in the form of suitable policy measures. In this regard, the
Sub-Committee draws the attention of the Government to the issues of price and purchase preference to BHEL,
and import duty concessions to the foreign companies. Though, in some cases price and purchase preference is
granted to the PSUs, the positive results of this measure are negated by the import duty concessions extended to
the foreign companies by the Government. These concessions and exemptions are precisely the reasons for the
playing field not being level for domestic companies or for that matter PSUs as the bids offered by foreign
players are much lower in comparison to the ones offered by PSUs. In other words, the competition is killed well
before it begins. The Sub-Committee believes that the need of the hour is not to go back to the days of
protectionism rather to provide a level playing field to all the players for the sake of  healthy competition.
 
               In view of the above, the Sub-Committee has come to the conclusion that the Government should take
necessary policy measures to extend 15%  price and purchase preference to BHEL vis-à-vis its bids for domestic
power projects. It also recommends that the Government should review its policy of giving duty concessions to
the foreign companies inasmuch as it leads to disadvantages to the domestic companies especially the PSUs. It is
the considered view of the Sub-Committee that foreign companies should not be shown favour at the expense of
domestic companies.

Ministry of Commerce declined the proposal of this ministry to restore refund of Terminal Excise
Duty(TED) in EXIM Policy 1999- 2000, as these benefits are directly related to the incidence of Custom
Duty(CD) and Counter-veiling Duty(CVD) on the imports for the project, i.e. whenever the imports are
exempted from the incidence of CVD, the domestic supplier is given the benefit of refund of TED. In die budget
2000-2001, in respect of power projects other than mega- power projects. fertilizer projects and refineries, CVD
has been increased to 16% and therefore the benefit of refund of TED is withdrawn for such projects.
 
A meeting was held by the Finance Secretary on 26.7.2000 to discuss the issue regarding the
competitiveness of Domestic Industries. As a follow up of this meeting, a note highlighting the following three
issues which are adversely affecting the domestic Industries was circulated to the concerned Ministries/
Departments by the Department of Revenue:-
 
(i)

 Applicability of withdrawal of refund of TED for contracts finalised before31.03.2000
 
(iii)        Rescindment of Customs Notification No. 85/99-CUS dated  06.07.99    permitting imports at
zero duty by projects funded by International organisations.
 
After analysing the views expressed by the various concerned Departments, Department of Revenue
summarised the position and recommended to this Ministry to take up the issues with TRU and DGFT.
 
Accordingly, the issue regarding restoration of TED for contracts finalised before 31.3.2000 was taken
up with DGFT. DGFT have since replied that the changes effected in the policy will be applicable in respect of
supplies effected from 1.4.2000 irrespective of whether LOI was opened prior to 31.3.2000 or after 31.3.2000.

COMMITTEE’S OBSERVATION
 
            Keeping in view the special role played by BHEL to the economy of the country and to enable it to face
the on-slaught of the foreign companies , the Committee recommended earlier that the Government should take
necessary policy measures to extend 15 % Purchase   Preference to BHEL  for International competitive  bids 
funded by multilateral funding agencies for domestic power projects.  The Committee also felt that foreign
companies should not  be shown favour at the expense of domestic companies.  The Committee now
recommends that the Ministry of Finance should take early dicision in respect of rescindment  of Custom
Notification No.85/9/CUS  dated 6-7-99  which allows import at  zero duty and DGFT should consider, as
special case, to issue notification for refund of terminal excise duty for projects ordered/bids under International 
Competitive  Bidding  prior to 1.4.2000.
 
The Committee is given  to understand that prior to 31.3.2000, domestic manufactures had secured
orders for projects and bids under International Competitive Bidding by passing on to the customer the benefit of
Refund of Terminal Excise Duty as applicable in the extant EXIM Policy. In the EXIM Policy announced on
31.3.2000, this benefit has been withdrawn. This may not impact short  duration projects,  but in case of long
duration power projects, where the cycle time for completion is normally 3-4 years, the schedule for supply of
capital goods is invariably 2-3 years. In all such contracts, Excise Duty (ED) is charged extra over and  above
the basic price of the equipment. Since this ED was refundable to the manufacturer, it was not indicated in the
price settled with customers. However, with the withdrawal of this refund, the 16% ED being quite substantial,
cannot be expected to be absorbed by the manufacturer. However, since the customers have frozen their project
cost and the financing structure based on the settled price and obtained approvals of competent/statutory
authorities, they are also not prepared to re-open their books    and accept  this additional duty burden.   In  such
a situation,  where customers are neither agreeable   to  re-negotiate the prices   to  compensate  the

(Annexure).

46th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/46threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:12:24]
 
 
II.         Background Of MoU System
 
2.1       The Department of Public Enterprises in their Background Note on the MoU system have stated that as a major
policy initiative, the MoU system was introduced by the Central Government as an important tool to improve the
performance of the Central Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs).  The New Industrial Policy of 1991 laid greater emphasis
on the MoU system requiring all PSEs to be brought under the ambit of the MoU system.  Beginning with 4 PSEs in
1987-88, the MoU system has now been extended to a large number of PSEs during the course of time and during the
year 2000-2001, 108 PSEs have signed the MoUs (Annexure).
 
2.2       It was stated that the main objectives of the MoU system are to improve the performance of the PSEs by
imparting increased autonomy and accountability and to provide a method of evaluation of the performance of the
managements of the PSEs in an objective and transparent manner.  Further, the objective of providing clarity of goals to
be achieved by PSEs is another dimension of the MoU system.
 
2.3       The Committee has noted that there is a High Power Committee (HPC) at the apex level, headed by the Cabinet
Secretary which is basically a policy making body for the MoUs.  This HPC consists of Secretaries of all nodal
Departments of Government such as Finance, Expenditure, Planning Commission and Programme Implementation, etc. 
The HPC undertakes the evaluation of the performance of the PSEs and in addition the HPC also provides a forum to
resolve inter-ministerial issues.
 
2.4       To assist HPC in this task and also to provide the technical inputs and to finalise the MoUs, there is an Advisory
Body called Adhoc Task Force (ATF), it was stated.  The members of the ATF are drawn from various fields having
vast experience in their areas and include retired Secretaries, Chief Secretaries, top experts in different disciplines like
finance, management, science and technology, and prominent academicians.   This body provides the neutrality and
objectivity to the MoU system.
 
2.5       The Department have also informed that under the present set up there is a small MoU Division under the
Department of Public Enterprises, Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises, which co-ordinates the entire
exercise of finalising the MoUs in respect of all the PSEs numbering 108. In addition to finalising the MoUs, the MoU
Division is also responsible for the evaluation of performance of PSEs, both on the basis of the provisional results as
well as the audited results.
 
2.6       Explaining about the process of preparing MoUs, the Department have stated that the MoU process starts with
the issuing of guidelines by the DPE to the PSEs/Administrative Ministries for drafting the MoUs.  The PSEs prepare
their MoUs on the basis of these guidelines and these draft MoUs are then discussed with the Administrative Ministries
and in the Boards of the PSEs and are then submitted to the DPE.  DPE prepares background papers and its comments
on each draft MoU keeping in view the past performance of the PSE, its future potential, the industry scenario and the
economic environment of the PSE, it was added.  It was further stated that these draft MoUs are discussed in the MoU

and the representatives from nodal Government Agencies like Ministry of Finance, Ministry of Statistics and
Programme Implementation and Planning Commission are also present.  The MoUs and the targets are finalised in these
meetings through mutual discussions.

VIII.     General Discussion
 
8.1       During the examination of MoUs signed by various PSUs with their Administrative Ministries, the Sub-
Committee  noticed that no weightage has been given to inter-PSU cooperation in the MoU.  It was felt that in the new
economic scenario, the collaborative approach amongst the PSUs under various ministries should be evolved without
compromising the competitive spirit and quality.
 
8.2       Besides, these PSUs should be given enough elbow room to adapt themselves in accordance with the new
realities.  They need an impetus for sustaining their work order position.  This could be addressed through inter-PSU
collaborative approach.  In this approach it is imperative that the PSUs and State Departments who enjoy client status
and those PSUs who are supplying their products/services to these PSUs should interact on a frequent and regular basis
from design, production to delivery stage.
 
8.3       This shall not only ensure a better coordinated and healthy relationship between these PSUs but also address
issues of better responsiveness, better quality of product, better degree of adherence to delivery schedules and cost
effectiveness.  This will also in a way encourage R&D efforts of the supplier PSUs enabling them to upgrade and update
their products, services and technologies to the needs of the client PSUs and Departments.

OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS AT A GLANCE
 
After considering all the issues that have arisen out of the examination of MoU System by the Sub-Committee,
the Committee is emphatic that Government should explore the ways and means for  bringing the element of inter-PSU
cooperation in the MoU system.
 
            The Committee further suggests that:
1.         In the case of domestic projects, where a consortium approach is called for, and one of the telecom PSUs is the
front end, it can invite, in the first instance, other concerned telecom PSUs to be consortium partners, on the basis of
right of first refusal.
 
2.         In the case of foreign contracts where TCIL is the front end and it is to either arrange for consortium partners or
arrange for suppliers, it can invite, in the first instance, the concerned telecom PSUs to participate on the basis of right
of first refusal.
 
3.         With reference to various supplies and contracts, there is an increasing emphasis on suppliers or buyers credit at
competitive rates.  In this context, the Exim Bank be persuaded to review its policies and procedures so that its terms
and conditions, including rates of interest are in line with the competitive best available in the International market.
 
4.         There have been persistent efforts by various Departments with the Finance Ministry to correct the duty
structure.  With the liberalisation, the duties on the finished goods have come down faster than the duties on the raw
materials in electronic and information technology.  If the duty structure is not corrected, the people will find import of
manufactured goods cheaper.  There should be a margin for conversion cost between the finished goods and the raw
materials.  The committee, therefore, suggests that the duty for finished goods should not go down than what is required.
 

46th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/46threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:12:24]
5.         The Sub-Committee in its deliberations gathered that there are instructions that for import purpose services of
agents are to be avoided.  But if one wants to sell something abroad, he needs an agent.  So, while PSUs have been told
to attune themselves with time, terms and conditions are not so dynamic as to make the agenda really interesting in
selling their goods abroad.  The Committee, therefore, suggests that Government should look into this aspect as well. 
Besides, our Missions abroad should have some sort of trade desk to explore the possibilities of having trade etc. with
the foreign countries.
 
6.         Last but not the least, under the present scenario of stiff competition from private and global companies, the
DPE should strengthen the MoU system specially where issues involving inter-ministerial/ inter PSU co-ordination are
concerned. The DPE should play a pro-active role in making the PSUs competitive and strengthening them for sustained
growth.
 
7.         The MoU system has undeniably made a positive contribution to improve the performance of the PSEs.  The
management of PSEs were appreciative of the fact that the MoU system has, for the first time brought about clarity of
the goals to be achieved on the basis of precise targets laid down in the MoU ensuring accountability on an objective
basis.  They were also enthusiastic of the larger delegation of powers available to the MoU signing Companies.  The
managements of the PSEs could act freely to a great extent with clear-cut objectives and goals.  Especially in their day-
to-day operations, the interference by the Ministries had reduced to a considerable extent. This has provided an
opportunity to the managements to take quick decisions and furthermore, evaluation of their performance is now being
done in a very objective and transparent basis.
 
8.         The Committee also feels that through the MoU system, an effort has been made to synthesise different
objectives.  Under the MoU system the parameters selected as performance indicators are a good mix of financial,
dynamic and efficiency indicators.  Thus, it is not only the financial parameters  which are given importance but other
dynamic and efficiency parameters  which are very essential for the future growth of the PSEs, and which are also
incorporated as performance indicators.  Thus, under the present system an attempt has been made to strike a balance
between financial and non-financial parameters.  The Committee is of the firm view that the MoU system has produced
reasonable results as it is understood that during the negotiation meetings an effort is made to set targets, which
represent an improvement over the level of performance in the previous year, and the system has significantly
contributed to a progressive increase in the performance of PSEs.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the MoU
system should continue on a long-term basis.
 
9.         Recently, the Public Sector Enterprises have been exposed to domestic and international competition.  Most of
them were operating in a totally protective environment.  With the policy of liberalisation and globalisation, the PSEs
have to compete in the market for obtaining orders both in products and services.  For a PSE to be competitive it is
essential to have an edge over its competitors, both in cost and quality.  In such a situation, the Committee feels that  up
gradation of technology including modernisation, up gradation of skills of employees and rationalisation of manpower
etc. are key factors to generate necessary competitive strength to PSEs.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
MoU system should be used as an effective instrument to bring about the change in the working environment of the
PSEs by introducing specific strategies through it to make them more competitive.
 
10.       The Committee observes that the role of the Ministries in the target setting exercise is very crucial but the work
relating to MoU system has not got the required attention of some of the Ministries due to various reasons.  The
concerned Ministries, therefore, need to play a greater role in the finalisation of MoU targets.
 
11.       Though the parameters such as preparation and implementation of corporate plan and devising a strategic plan or
vision plan, etc. are being mentioned in the MoU documents, the targets set in the MoUs do not often correspond to the
corporate vision/plans drawn up by the PSEs.  The Committee, therefore, stresses that there should be a better linkage
between the corporate plans of the PSEs and the MoUs.
 
12.       The Committee is constrained to note that the MoU preparation has generally been an annual target setting
exercise.  The Committee feels that the MoU system should focus on strategic issues rather than be a mere annual target
setting exercise.  For that purpose the Administrative Ministries should provide adequate input/support to enable PSEs
to develop future strategies in association with the Ministries.  The parameters under the MoU need to be devised
depending upon the strategy for its future growth in the particular area of its operations.  The performance of the PSEs
needs to be reviewed on the basis of parameters so devised.  This would give a clear picture as to how a particular PSE
has been able to make its products/services cost effective and how they compare with their counter parts in the private
sector.  Such an approach would certainly make the PSEs not only competitive but also provide an opportunity to
become global players.  Therefore, the Committee suggests that the approach under the MoU system needs to be
reviewed in line with the existing competitive economic environment.

46th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/46threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:12:24]
 
13.       As PSEs have to operate in a free market, they cannot continue to depend upon Government’s assistance on
matters such as obtaining orders, etc.  In the present situation, negotiating for orders is a managerial function and,
therefore, the Government’s  intervention should be very selective, if at all.  For instance, a number of the PSEs are
working in the same area but they are under the control of different administrative ministries.  In some cases, these PSEs
operate as competitors to each other.  Similarly, PSEs are also involved in research and development projects and some
of the PSEs are spending quite a significant aMoUnt on R&D activities.  Unfortunately, these PSEs are working in
isolation and there is no coordination to provide synergy in R&D, marketing, etc. to enhance their competitive edge over
their counter partners in the private sectors.  Since these PSEs are functioning in watertight compartments, they are not
able to reap the maximum benefits of their investments on R&D and up gradation of technology.  Separate and isolated
efforts on the part of the PSEs in such areas only result in addition to their costs.  Therefore, there is tremendous scope
in bringing together PSEs operating in the same discipline, but under different Ministries, to optimise investments in
marketing, R&D etc. in a collective and coordinated manner.  The Committee, therefore, feels that the Department of
Public Enterprises operating through the MoU system appears to be an appropriate forum where the issues involving
inter-ministries/inter-PSEs coordination can be taken up more effectively and DPE as a nodal Department should play a
more pro-active role in making the PSEs competitive and strengthening them for sustained growth.
 
14.       On the question of reduction of budgetary support to Department of Public Enterprises and its consequent
winding up in pursuance of recommendation of Expenditure Reforms Commission (EFC), it has not considered the
essentially vital role played by the  Department of Public Enterprises in making the Memoranda of Understanding which
the Government of India enters with its Public Sector Units on the annual basis.  The Department is merely not
facilitating but enabling the MoU to be an important tool for performance assessment mutates mutandis to that of Profit
Center Concepts of large Conglomerates in developed countries.  The MoU is an effective and objective tool today only
because of it being facilitated by a non-stakeholder that is Department of Public Enterprises.  Hence, the Committee
strongly feels that the Department of  Public Enterprises should be strengthened with budgetary support. 
 
15.       In the course of evaluation study of several MoUs  the Sub Committee also noted that many of the Public
Sectors Enterprises  are working in isolation.  A better synergetic approach with each Central Public Sector Enterprises
working in closer cooperation with other Public Sectors Enterprises will enable many of the Sick PSEs to come out of
the woods.  The Sub Committee felt that had any such mechanism been in existence the sickness in many Public Sector 
Enterprises could have been avoided especially in respect of those where the sickness can be attributed to lack of 
orders.  Moreover, a synergetic effort must be made in terms of joint bidding in respect of international offers, joint
effort to enable pre-qualification by giving them better access to larger market, cost competitiveness and also a joint
strategy in tackling sickness.  Hence the Committee strongly recommends that an Inter Public Sector Enterprises
Coordination Cell should also be established in the Department of Public Enterprises for providing a mechanism for
better  and cohesive cooperation amongst the Units Central Public Sector Enterprises.
 
 
16.       The Sub Committee during the course of its study of MoUs of many Public Sector Undertakings like Bharat
Electronics Limited, ITI Limited, HTL Limited, TCIL Limited, etc., observed that the products of these units are of high
quality and excellent potential exist for export  of these products.  However, there  is a need to facilitate this export
opportunity through better coordination, contract specific joint ventures etc.  The Department of Public Enterprises
could also be vested with this function of promoting  exports from these Central Public Sectors Enterprises.  The
Committee, therefore, recommends  for setting up of an Export Promotion Cell for Central Public Sectors in the
Department of Public Enterprises.
 
17.       The Committee observes that the strength of the MoU system is that the targets are finalised and the
performance of the PSE is evaluated in an objective and transparent manner that is ensured by the DPE and ATF.  Thus,
in order to maintain and further instil objectivity, the Committee feels that DPE should play a more active role in the
process and the MoU Division should be strengthened so that they can carry out bench marking studies, performance
related studies and other associated work so that the targets given to the PSEs are more realistic.
 
18.       The Committee is, however, constrained to note that the MoU Division of the Department of  Public Enterprises
has been proposed to be abolished.  The Secretary, Ministry of Heavy Industry and Public Enterprises, during the course
of his oral evidence before the Committee in connection with the Demands for Grants, informed the Committee that the
Expenditure Reforms Commission has recommended that the Department of Public Enterprises may be down-sized .  It
was proposed that  the  MoU System  may be transferred to the respective Administrative Ministries of the concerned
PSEs. The Committee, however, does not agree with this.   The Committee feels that the Department of Public
Enterprises provides a neutral forum for finalising MoUs  which is essential to make it an objective systems.  It is also
ensured that the entire MoU exercise is carried out in an objective, transparent and broad based manner.  The

Committee, therefore, recommends that instead of transferring the MoU System to the concerned Administrative
Departments, it may be retained with the Department of Public Enterprises. In fact the MoU Division needs to be further
strengthened for an effective implementation of the MoU System.

REPORT
 
I.          INTRODUCTION 
 
1.1       The Department of Heavy Industry is concerned with the development of the heavy engineering industry,
machine tool industry, heavy electrical industry, industrial machinery and auto-industry. The Industries covered by this
Department provide goods and services for almost all sectors of the economy, including power, rail and road transport.
They also cater to the requirements of equipments for basic industries such as steel, non-ferrous metals, fertilizers,
refineries, petrochemicals, shipping, textiles, paper, cement, sugar etc. The Department is responsible for development of
a wide range of intermediate engineering products like castings, forgings, diesel engines, industrial gears and gear boxes.
It is  also  vested with the administrative charge of 48 Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs).
 
1.2       The  PSEs under the administrative control of the Department are engaged in manufacturing of
engineering/capital goods, consultancy and contracting activities. The total investment (Gross Block) in 48 Public Sector
Enterprises under the Department was about Rs.7780.24 crores  till  March, 2000  employing about 1.61 lakh  persons.
 
1.3       The Department holds interactions with various industry councils and evolves plans for their growth. The
Department also assists Public Sector Enterprises through policy initiatives, resolution of problems relating to tariffs and
trade, technological collaboration, up- gradation and Research & Development, etc.

III.       RESEARCH & DEVELOPMENT OF AUTOMOTIVE INDUSTRY
 
3.1       The Department stated that R&D and technology development is the backbone of the automotive industry.
Because of this fact, a cess has been imposed on Automobiles with effect from 1.1.1984 and on tractors from 1.10.1985
at the rate of 18% ad-valorem to finance R&D in the industry. The cess is being collected by the Department of Revenue
and forms part of the Consolidated Fund of India. The Ministry of Finance is allocating a Portion of this fund through the
Budget to this Ministry under the head “Cess for the Development Council for Automobile and Allied Industries”.
 
3.2       It was also stated that with the fragmented automobile industry in India, it is not feasible for the individual units
to establish full-fledged R&D set up and testing facilitates. Hence there is a need to establish  R&D testing  facilities
which will cater  to the industry as a whole. With the  introduction of new and stricter emission norms as well as safety
standards , more & more  R&D facilities are needed in the country to meet the demand of the Industry, it was added. The
Department further added that the Development Council for Automotive and Allied Industry (DCAAI) allocates  Cess
funds for research and development to establish R&D institutions through a Cess Committee chaired by Secretary,
Department of  Heavy Industry. 
 
3.3       The Secretary during the course of his oral evidence informed the Committee that  there is tremendous need for
creating the testing facilities in the country as well as having R&D projects. He also informed the Committee that the
DHI have constituted the Development Council of Automotive Sector and  have established a Committee  to  authorize
and recommend use of R&D and testing facilities. The Secretary also mentioned to the Committee that  0.05% cess 

47th Report

may  not  be sufficient looking at the requirement of fund that has emerged.
              
3.4          It was further stated by the Secretary that in view of Euro II and Euro III norms,  considerable investment in
testing facilities will have to be generated, and also, DHI  have to provide for testing to see that the imported new and
old cars  conform to CMVR norms. Therefore, there is an added requirement for testing facilities, he felt. He also stated
that  there is a need now to set up at least two testing tracks, one in  the North and another in the South. In view of all
this, the cess needs to be raised to 0.25%, the Secretary felt.  It was revealed by the Secretary,  that the Department had
got Rs.10 crores for utilization from the Cess Fund which  is also insufficient. This will have to be considerably
increased if the DHI wants  to give fillip to R&D and testing facilities, he felt.
 
3.5       The Secretary also informed the Committee that there is need for promoting electric vehicles. He also felt that
there is need for having nominal custom and excise duties for electric vehicles and also for subsidy through the
Department of Non-Conventional Sources of Energy for three wheelers that they were giving for larger vehicles. 
 
3.6       The Committee  feels that the  cess  which  has been used till now for creating facilities for conducting test as per
Central Motor Vehicle Rules needs to be  used for  other areas  of product and process related research with a view to
giving a fillip to   India’s  automobile industries.  It is also necessary to enable the  automobile industries to survive   the 
imports  surge after WTO regime became fully applicable.  The  Committee  recommends that the Ministry should  take
stock of what is being done and what  further is to be done.  R&D  has  to be undertaken for product and process related
research also.
 
3.7       The Committee understands that the cess of 0.05%, which is being charged at  present, needs to be increased to
0.25% for  making   necessary investment in testing  facilities.  The Committee agrees with the view expressed by the
Secretary that the allocation of Rs. 10 crores, that  has been made, is insufficient  as R&D  and testing facilities  have to
be enhanced.  Therefore, Ministry of Finance may consider increasing at RE stage.
 
3.8       The Committee also  agrees  with the views expressed by the Secretary that the need of the hour is electric
vehicles for having pollution free transportation  in the cities, particularly, in the metropolises. The Government   may
consider exemption of customs duty and surcharge on items imported for use in manufacture of electric vehicles and
reduction of excise duty on electric vehicles. The Ministry of Non-Conventional  Sources of  Energy  may  also consider 
providing  subsidies to the extent of 50% to three  wheelers and the Department of Heavy Industry may  pursue the
matter in this regard.
 
3.9       The Department  have also  informed  the Committee that after  India  became  compliant with the WTO regime
with effect from 01-04-2001, quantitative restrictions on imports, regulations regarding local content in manufacture and
export obligations would  not be admissible. Import of automotive vehicles of all categories would  become permissible..
In order to address the following issues, the Ministry is in the process of formulating a comprehensive  holistic policy
compatible with the WTO regime:-
(i)
                  Exalt the sector as a lever of industrial growth and employment.
(ii)                Promote a globally competitive automotive industry and emerge as a global source for auto
components.
(iii)               Enable the development of a domestic safety and environmental regulatory structure for the
sector.
(iv)              Facilitate indigenous design, research and development.
 
3.10     The Committee  feels that the policy compatible with  WTO regime should have been formulated  much   before 
the regime became fully operational.  At least now, there should not be any further delay in formulating the Policy.

XIV.  GENERAL PROBLEMS OF PAPER INDUSTRY
 
14.1     Newsprint industry has been traditionally at a disadvantageous position due to lower return on its capital
employed, causing investments to go to higher returnable sectors. The opportunity costs entailed due to the above
scenario could have been obviated by appropriate policy instrument. However, abolition of QRs as a result of WTO
commitment has hit the newsprint harder and the 1:2 procurement condition now will have to be disbanded. Also, other
non-tariff barriers also have caused to be removed leading to inclusion of newsprint under the Open General License. In
this scenario the only ray of light to enable this industry to survive or turn-around is through the systematic tariff regime.
However, it is observed that a progressive and systematic tariff regime has been denied to this industry.  While the bound
rate under the WTO is 35%, the customs duty at present is at 5%. Besides, many of the intermediaries used in the 
manufacture of newsprint also attract very high custom duty rates. This type of customs tariff structure is not
commensurate with the fiscal logic, which accords higher custom duty on end products than the intermediaries. 
 
14.2     Hence, the Committee recommends that the Government may not only consider raising the custom’s duty to the
WTO bound level but also a TARIFF REALIGNMENT exercise may be taken up by the government to enable this
industry  to be accorded a level playing field for realizing higher productivity.
 
14.3     The Committee also observed that the industry has been recently putting a lot of efforts towards replenishment of
critical forests, which are used in newsprint products. This replenishment effort of the industry should be strongly
supported by the government not only to ensure present ecological balance but also as a futuristic measure. The
Committee hence strongly recommends that a proactive support be extended to the industry  in terms of relaxing or
expediting the necessary administrative clearance for this noble exercise of the industry.
 
14.4     During the course of examination of Demands for Grants of Ministry of Heavy Industry,  the performance review
of HPC and NEPA  mills, the Committee observed certain anomalies in the excise/customs tariff classification of papers
and paperboards. The paper and paperboards are classified under the same heading. It is felt that while the end products
are distinctly different, even the manufacturing process involved is also different. The paperboard is made out of waste
recycling through non-conventional source and needs to be classified differently from paper, which, inter-alia, should
cover newsprint papers, etc. In this context it also came to the light that there is an excise duty exemption availed by
paper and newspaper manufacturers as well as paper board manufacturers producing upto 3500 MT annually. During the
investigation,  it came to the light of the committee that the mills are operating at sub-optimal capacity restricting their
production to 3500 MTs, enabling them to avail of this excise duty exemption.
 
14.5     The Committee  recommends that this anomaly needs to be corrected through distinguishing paper from
paperboard by virtue of differently classifying or sub-classifying one product from another. As regards duty exemption,
it is felt that the same should be based on installed capacity of the units and not annual production as such a provision is
vulnerable to abuse resulting in sub-optimal utilization of the capacity by units, which can also, amongst other things,
cause potential shortages of the products resulting in upward trend in prices of boards. 
 
14.6     The CMD, HNL informed the Committee that the quality of the imported newsprint from Canada is definitely
superior to our newsprint in terms of brightness. The price difference is about  Rs. 3000 per tonne. The advantage that
the countries like Canada, Europe, etc., have got is that they are having superior raw materials like spruce, pine, etc.,
where they can go in for lower g.s.m. newsprint. Now, every newspaper  publisher  wants to pay by weight and print by
metre. Newspaper publishing houses want to install machines which can print 1 lakh copies per hour, 40 pages at a time.
They are all going for high speed printing machines. With the kind of raw materials we are having in our country, we
will not be able to catch up to  that level, he added. To that extent, a lot of R&D is required to be done and the R&D
efforts are being done through the Central Pulp and Paper Research Institute,  in a modest way by the newspaper
manufacturers.
 
14.7     The Committee feels that the R&D efforts being made to improve the quality of newsprint are not to the extent it
is necessary. Looking at the present scenario, it  is very essential to catch-up with the best technology. Therefore, the

year of revival package i.e., 1999-2000, the company recorded a substantial growth in production from Rs.217 crs. In
(1998-99) to Rs.784 crs. In (1999-2000) signifying an increase of 260%.
 
21.4        The Department have also  stated that the Government approved a package of assistance together with capital
restructuring which, inter-alia, included reservation of orders. The package of assistance together with financial
restructuring for Hindustan Cables Limited was approved by the Cabinet on 27.1.99.  With the availability of orders
under the package of assistance, the company achieved production of 85.43 LCKM of Jelly Filled Cables and 46860
FKM of Optical Fibre Cables during the year 1999-2000.  The Turnkey Project Division achieved a turnover of Rs. 218
crores.  Overall the Company achieved turnover of Rs. 803.51 crores during 1999-2000 registering 350% growth over
the actual of Rs. 222.31 crores during 1998-99.
 
21.5        The Department also stated that after providing for interest and depreciation, the net loss came down to Rs.
39.32 crores from a level of Rs. 138.73 crores during the previous year 1998-99, also the net loss for the year 1999-2000
could be contained at a level of Rs. 39.32 crores as against Rs. 50.51 crores projected at the end of the first year of
implementation of the package.  In the current year 2000-01 the company has achieved a turnover of Rs. 592.18 crores
as against Rs.501.43 crores in the corresponding period previous year thereby registering a growth of 18%.  The
estimated net loss from April, 2000 to December, 2000 is Rs. 49.97 crores.   HCL has been provided a budget support of
Rs.13.50 crores in BE-2001-2002.
 
21.6     The Committee feels that orders for its products from other PSEs and Govt. agencies  is an essential requirement
to enable the company to show upward graph. The Committee notes that DoT has reserved 25% of its requirement for
HCL.The Committee, however, realises that the limited orders placed to H.C.L. by other sister concerns in Govt. sector
is not enough to make the company viable. The Committee, therefore, recommends that Government  should help the
company in exploring market in the private sector as well as foreign countries with help of TCIL.
 
21.7     The Committee came to know that the company is having problem for taking loan from banks on higher rate of
interest which is eating into its profit which they have earned after putting valiant effort. The Committee recommends
that Govt. should stretch its helping hand to the company to sort out the problem in every possible manner.

I.          INTRODUCTION
 
1.1       The Department of Public Enterprises acts as a nodal agency for all PSEs and assists in policy formulation pertaining
to the policy guidelines on performance improvement and evaluation, financial accounting, personnel management and in
related areas. It also collects, evaluates and maintains information on several areas in respect of PSEs. In fulfilling its roles  it
associates itself with other Ministries and Organizations.
 
1.2
              The important   role  and  tasks of  the Department  of  Public  Enterprises  are:-
 
(i)        General policy relating to Public Sector Enterprises;
(ii)       Matters relating to issue of Presidential Directives and Guidelines to    Public Sector Enterprises;
(iii)      Formulation of Policy Guidelines pertaining to Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs) in areas like performance
improvement and evaluation, financial   management, personnel management, board structures, wage
settlement, training, industrial relation, vigilance, performance appraisal, etc.;
(iv)     All matters relating to Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between the    Public    Sector Enterprises and
the Administrative Ministries / Departments.;
(v)       Matters relating to  the delegation of powers to Board of Directors;
(vi)     To undertake in-depth studies in respect of significant areas of functioning of central PSEs.;
(vii)Matters relating to International Centre for Promotion of Enterprises (ICPE);
(viii)     Matters relating to Standing Conference of Public Enterprises (SCOPE);
(ix)     To monitor and evaluate the performance of PSEs and to act as a repository of data and to bring out an
Annual Survey for the Parliament; and
(x)    Permanent Machinery of Arbitrators for settlement of   disputes among   Public Sector Enterprises and
Government Departments except disputes      relating to tax  matters.
1.3      The Department has five constituent Divisions, viz,  the Financial Policy Division, the Management Policy Division,
the MOU Division, the Administration & Coordination  Division and Permanent Machinery of Arbitration. The Financial
Policy Division comprises the Public Enterprises Survey Unit, the Policy Planning Unit, and the Wage Policy Unit. The
Management Policy Division comprises the personnel policy unit, training unit, performance indicator and work norms unit
(PIWN Unit) and SC & ST Cell. The MOU Division comprises MOU Unit, Data Bank and Computer Cell. The
Administration & Coordination Division comprises the Administration, Library, Parliament and Coordination Wings and
Hindi Cell. The Permanent Machinery of Arbitration (PMA) provides a forum for settlement of commercial disputes
between two or more PSEs as well as between a Government Department and PSEs.

2.6       As already stated earlier the Department of Public Enterprises  acts as  a nodal agency for all PSEs and assists in policy
formulation pertaining to the role of PSEs in the Economy. The Department strives for professionalisation of PSEs , providing
operational and financial autonomy, making PSEs accountable, infusing transparency in management, achieving managerial
excellence and increasing productivity.
2.7       When asked about  the steps taken by the Government to strengthen the Department, it was  stated  that  the
Department of Public Enterprises  was mainly  a facilitating  Department which lays down ground rules  for functioning of 
PSEs.  The  Department  monitors  the  performance   of  the PSEs and submits its reports  periodically to the Cabinet. It
reviews  performance of these PSUs and specific  objectives in the light of MOU signed by them.   The  Department  has  been
performing  these functions ever since it was established as the   Bureau   of    Public    Enterprises  in   the    sixties. 
However, the role of  DPE with  regard to  Disinvestment  has  been limited after the creation of separate Department of 
Disinvestment (DOD). The only significant change that has taken place is that all  the parliamentary  matters which were
earlier being    handled either by DPE or Ministry of Finance  with regard to disinvestments are now being dealt by  DOD.  It
was also stated that even after  the creation of separate Department of Disinvestment, the Department of Public Enterprises
would  continue to be the nodal Department  for formulating general policy  relating to Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs) and
for finalisation of the Memorandum of Understanding signed  between the Public Sector Enterprises and the Administrative
Ministries.
 
2.8       It was also stated  that  the staff strength of DPE at different levels was reduced substantially.  A 10% cut was  effected
in the sanctioned strength as a part of economy measures in 1996. Thus, review and  rationalisation of the working strength
has always been an ongoing  feature process.  It may be mentioned that DPEs working strength was reduced from 262 in 1985
to the present 136 over a period of time.
2.9         The Committee is of the view that the present staff strength numbering about 136 of the Department of  Public
Enterprises needs to be increased in view of the wide roles and functions being undertaken by the department. The Department
needs to be strengthened.
 
III.       SEARCH COMMITTEE AND NAVRATNAS &   MINIRATNAS
 
3.1       The Ministry stated that a  Search Committee is set up with the approval of the Cabinet for selecting   non-official part
time Directors for Navratna and Miniratna PSUs.The Search Committee selects non-official part time Directors of impeccable
stature and background for induction of at least 4 non-official Directors in the case of Navratna PSEs and 3 non-official
Directors in the case of Miniratna PSEs.  Non-official part time Directors are drawn from Public men, Technocrats,
Management Experts & Consultants and Professional Managers in Industry & Trade with high degree of proven ability.  They
play a complimentary role in providing professional and managerial advice to the Board and are appointed with the approval
of ACC on part time basis.
 
3.2       Professionalisation of the Boards of Public Enterprises  is one of the thrust areas of Public Sector Reforms as it is vital
to the functioning of the Board and in achieving high standards of performance. Detailed instructions in this regard were

issued vide DPE O.M. No.18(6)/91-GM dated 16.3.1992. Non-official Directors can play an important role in formulation of a
Company’s strategy and in ensuring that the Board sets its sights high enough. Their contribution to strategy is often through
asking well directed questions, critically but constructively.
 
3.3       The Boards of these PSEs have been broad based by appointment of part-time non-official directors. These
enterprises, subject to certain guidelines,  enjoy freedom to make capital expenditure, enter into joint ventures, effect
organizational restructuring, create and wind up of posts below Board level, raise capital from the domestic and international
markets, establish financial joint ventures subject to equity investments with specified limits etc.
3.4        The Government have also granted enhanced financial, managerial and    operational  autonomy to other profit-
making enterprises, called Miniratnas. These enterprises should have earned profits continuously for the three previous years,
have positive net worth, did not seek budgetary support or guarantees from the Government and   have not   defaulted in the  
repayment of   loans/interests to the Government. These enterprises can incur capital expenditure, enter into joint ventures, set
up technological and strategic alliances, formulate schemes of human resources management, etc. subject to certain
stipulations and guidelines.
3.5        The Committee, however, would like to know  how far  such an  enlarged  Board of Directors  consisting of  official
/non-officials/part time Directors has produced the desired  results .  The Committee feels that  the Department of  Public
Enterprises should undertake  a study in the matter. 
 
3.6       It was also stated  that the grant  of Navratna and Miniratna  status was one time affair meaning thereby once the status
of Navratna or Miniratna had been accorded to a PSU it remains with it  forever notwithstanding the subsequent upheaval in
its  performance.
3.7       The Committee has been informed that the Department of Public Enterprises  confers  Navratna status to the identified
central PSEs, which have comparative advantages to become global giants.  The accordance of Navratna status to Central
PSEs is done in consultation with the concerned administrative Ministries after obtaining approval of the Cabinet.
 
3.8       The Department have further informed that there are 11 Navratnas and 46 Miniratnas . It was further informed that the
procedures for accordance of Navratna status to the enterprises and also for divestment of such status have been referred to the
Group of Ministers.  Final decision is yet to be taken.
 
3.9       The Committee, however, feels that  the Department of  Public Enterprises  should review the performance  of such 
companies in order to  know  whether  such companies are maintaining the status for  which there were awarded such
elevated  positions. The Committee feels that the procedure to accord the Navratna status is a tardy procedure which needs to
be revised by the Government. Secondly, the responsibility of  accordance of the status of Miniratna, presently being  held  by
the respective  administrative ministries themselves to the concerned PSE, must be transferred to the Search Committee under
the Department of Public Enterprises.

V.        THE PURCHASE PREFERENCE POLICY
 
5.1       The Government on the 14
th September, 2000 decided to extend the Purchase Preference Policy for products and services of
central PSEs for two years i.e. up to 31.3.2002.
The main rationale of continuing Purchase Preference Policy and its objectives are as under :
 
a.
                   Some of PSEs are still passing through a period of transition;
b.                  Restructuring and adjustment with new economic environment is in process;
c.                   The turnaround of many sick and loss making PSEs and survival of marginally profit making PSEs is dependent on
their securing adequate order book. 
 
5.2       The Committee has been informed that  this policy has been of immense assistance in this endeavour.The Purchase
Preference Policy has greatly assisted PSEs in withstanding the competition in the market.  Central PSEs to a great extent have been
able to avail the benefit of Purchase Preference Policy by utilising their capacities. The Notice Inviting Tender in each case is 
required  to  specify  provisions  of  purchase  preference  as per DPE’s OM dated 14.9.2000 . The Secretary agreed that some Public
Sector Enterprises are not following guidelines and are not specifying  this  provision in their Notice Inviting Tenders.  
 
5.3       The Committee agrees that the policy of Purchase Preference has been of immense assistance for the PSEs and  has greatly
assisted PSEs in withstanding the competition in the present consumer economy. The  Central PSEs to great extent have been able to
avail the benefit of Purchase Preference Policy by utilising their capacities.  The Committee is ,however, constrained to note that the 
Government of India  on the 14
th September, 2000 decided to extend the Purchase Preference Policy for products and services of
Central PSEs for two years  only i.e. up to 31.3.2002.
 
5.4       The Committee recommends that   the Purchase Preference Policy should be extended  for another  3 years , i.e,. upto 
31.3.2004.
 
5.5       The Committee in this connection would like to place on record that the Minister of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises
has recently brought out a Brochure  indicating the highlights and the achievements of the Public Sector Undertakings (Annexture-I).
The Minister has in the brochure  indicated that the Public Sector has played a pivotal role in the industrial and economic
development of the country.  The growth in Public Sector Enterprises has been noteworthy, the Minister indicated.  He has further
stated that the government is committed to reform and restructure the public sector enterprises so that they stand poised with the best
of their kind in the world.
 
5.6       The Committee is very much concerned to note that  certain Central PSEs/Central Govt. Agencies are not including the
Purchase Preference clause in their Notice Inviting Tender (NIT) depriving the other Central PSEs to avail the benefit of the
Government Policy.   This non-cooperative attitude of some of the PSEs does not go well with the overall policy of the government 
to improve the health of  PSEs.  The highlights indicated by the Minister would remain only highlights  without a major shift in their
health status.  If there has to be a major reversal in the health condition of the PSEs, all the PSEs need to have mutual cooperation. 
Purchase Preference Policy is one such gray area which, if followed scrupulously by all the PSUs, would improve the performance of
all the ailing PSEs.
 
5.7       The Committee, therefore, recommends that all the Administrative Ministries/Government Departments should issue the
instructions to the PSEs under their jurisdiction to comply with the policy of the Government on Purchase Preference. 
5.8       The Committee also recommends that the Department of Public Enterprises should ensure and  monitor the compliance of the
Purchase Preference Policy. In this regard all Public Sector Enterprises may be asked to submit documents of NIT to the Department
of Public Enterprises for regular compliance.

VI.    MEMORANDUM OF UNDERSTANDING
6.1       Under  the present set-up of the Department of Public Enterprises, the MoU Division is one of the five constituent
Divisions of the Department of Public Enterprises which co-ordinates the entire exercise of finalizing the Memorandum of 
Understandings  (MoUs) in respect of all the Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) numbering about 108.  The New
Industrial Policy of 1991 laid greater emphasis of the MoU system requiring all PSEs to be brought under the ambit of the
MoU system.
6.2       With the advent of the privatization and globalisation in Indian Economy mainly after the implementation of  New
Industrial Policy of 1991, the Central PSEs have been exposed to the domestic and international competition. Now, these 
PSEs  have   to   compete  with  the    Private  Sector  in   the   consumer  economy. In such a stiff competitive environment, it
is essential for a PSE to have an edge of both cost and quality over its competitors. MoU system has been accepted by the
PSEs as a panacea  since it has given them more freedom to take decisions independently  and operate more effectively and
proficiently.
 
6.3     The Government of India following the recommendation of the Arjun Sengupta Committee introduced the MOU
system. The MOU system has grown at a steady rate and from 4 MOUs signed in the year 1987-88  it has grown to  108 PSEs
which have  signed MoUs for the year 1999-2000.
 
6.4       The main objective of the MOU system was to improve the performance of the PSEs through the mechanism of
increased autonomy and accountability and also to provide a uniform method of evaluation of the performance of the
managements of the PSEs in an objective and transparent manner. Further, it was also envisaged to provide a clarity of
goals/objectives to be achieved by PSEs.
6.5       The purpose of the MOU system are to :
 
(i)
      Measure the performance of PSEs taking into account the complexity of fusing social and financial objectives
and translating them into measurable parameters:
(ii)    Ensure simultaneous increase in autonomy as well as accountability;
(iii)   Set up new institutions and administrative & personnel systems;
(iv)  Replace `multiple principles with multiple objectives’ with clarity in goals and objectives;
(v)    Break the vicious circle of NOT ME syndrome.
 
6.6       The Department of Public Enterprises provides a neutral forum for finalising the MOUs which is essential to make it
an objective system. The Department provides the entire technical and analytical inputs such as preparation of the common
guidelines for drafting of MOUs, preparation of background notes and critiques on the draft MOUs submitted by the PSEs,
Organisation of MOU negotiation and evaluation meetings, etc., of the expert group called Ad-Hoc Task Force(ATF) in order
to finalise the MOUs and evaluate the performance of the PSEs at the end of the year. Department of Public Enterprises
ensures that the entire MOU exercise is carried out in an objective, transparent and broad based manner.
 
6.7       It acts as the permanent  secretariat to the HPC and ATF. The main functions of the MoU Division are:
·
        To provide logistical support to the Ad-Hoc Task Force.  It is expected to provide not only administrative
support but also technical support to the Ad-Hoc Task Force.
·        To act as buffer between the Ad-Hoc  Task  Force  members and the   signatories to  the MoUs, i e,  PSEs   and
Administrative  Ministries .  It is  expected  that ATF   members will have contacts with signatories to MoU 
through  MoU Division only.
·        To  develop information and data base on various PSEs signing MoU.
·        To  prepare agenda and background papers for the  High Power Committee.
·        To monitor the progress of  the MoUs.  The MoU  Division keeps a watch  on various stages involving in the
preparation of MoUs to ensure that all parties involved in the process adhere to the relevant  guidelines and
deadlines.
·        To  provide advice  and counsel to the MoU signatories on methodological and conceptual aspects  of the
MoU  Policy.
·        To coordinate research  and training on various aspects  of MoU Policy.
 
6.8       During the oral evidence , Secretary, Department of Public Enterprises, informed the Committee that  expenditure 
reforms  commission have recommended that the work relating to the preparation and evaluation of MoU could be left  to the
